noi_dung:
Audio Links at http://www.phatphaponline.org

Why is everyone in a state of delusion? Because they do not understand where they come from or where they go when they die. The figure you see each day when you look in the mirror is not you. If you want to know your original face (your true mind), you must turn the light around and look into your own mind; seek it in your own mind. Worldly people are deluded by the five desires: day after day they are gripped and stifled by money, beauty, fame, food, and sleep, yet they still willingly resign themselves to being slaves to these things.

Our greed is higher than heaven and thicker than earth. It is like a bottomless bucket: no matter how much you pour in, it never fills.

Only those without virtue and morality are truly poor and destitute.

Where can you find the jewels and treasures you already possess? Look in the Flower Adornment Sutra. There is a saying: "If you have not read the Flower Adornment Sutra, you cannot know the riches of the Buddhas." The Flower Adornment Sutra is the king of all kings of sutras (the foremost among the most wonderful sutras spoken by the Buddha).

If you handle all matters with greed, anger, and delusion, the result is that heaven and earth will darken and disasters of every kind will arise. If you solve problems with morality, samadhi, and wisdom, heaven and earth will be bright and clear, and all will be auspicious. Thus it is said: where there are many evil people, there are many disasters; where there are many good people, there is lasting peace and joy. Calamity or peace all come from people.

People fail to become Buddhas because they only apply effort at the mouth (talking without cultivating, without practicing).

Everything, every matter, is the Buddhadharma — all things that cannot be grasped or clung to. In this world, everything that happens, every single thing, is itself proclaiming the Dharma (revealing the truth); it is itself lecturing the sutra. Each of us should take the sutra of our own life, read it carefully, learn it by heart, and never act against the principle of cause and effect. Our very life is the truest sutra of all.

If you keep seeing other people's faults, you are still suffering. Once you have ended suffering, you will see everyone as a Buddha. Whoever you look at, you will see as a Buddha. It is so simple, so plain — yet you cannot do it!

People do not live in order to eat. To live means to render service to the world, to be virtuous toward others, to benefit all under heaven. We must: With compassion, teach on Heaven's behalf; with loyalty and filial devotion, rescue the people for the nation.

A day without correcting your faults is a day without creating merit and virtue.

Affliction is itself enlightenment (bodhi): that is, right in the moment affliction arises, if you can refrain from giving rise to affliction, if you can recognize it for what it is, then that very moment is called enlightenment. It is not a matter of throwing affliction away and then going off to find some other enlightenment elsewhere.

The AIDS epidemic is a disease of genocide, a disease that destroys nations. I hope the Chinese people will not wish to lose their country, and will not imitate the conduct of Westerners.

Those who study the Buddhadharma must restrain their desires, keep their minds pure, and want little. They should not harbor many desires. This is essential, for it is the very root of good health.

That you have been able to take refuge in the Triple Jewel today is because in the past you planted great and wholesome roots. Now that we are gathered here, the whole assembly should bring forth the resolve for enlightenment (bodhicitta) and seek the unsurpassed Way. Do not be parasites in Buddhism; do not be rotten, depraved elements. If you see someone slandering Buddhism, do not argue with them. Cultivate with solid, genuine practice. Use your cultivation to make the Buddha's teaching shine. Do not use lip-service (mouth Zen) to win their faith. You must truly cultivate.

Wars in the world all begin with the tiny wars that start in our own minds. The ancients said: The rise or fall of a nation is the responsibility of every ordinary person. You should not think: "That is other people's business, not mine." If everyone were without warfare in the mind, then wars in the world would cease.

Do not shine the light outward. At all times you must turn the light around and shine it upon your own mind. Look and see: are you an animal? A ghost? What are you?

What is virtue and morality? It is taking the benefit of living beings as one's aim, and taking non-obstruction of others as one's principle. Virtue and morality also mean a heart filled with kindness, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and good faith.

Why are we not in accord with the Way? Because the mad mind has not yet stopped. (The mad mind is the mind full of false thoughts.)

Good deeds begin in the mind. Evil deeds also begin in the mind.

The three poisons of greed, anger, and delusion are far more potent than opium, strong liquor, or the deadliest poison. Drugs, liquor, and poisons are only visible toxins that harm the body. But greed, anger, and delusion harm our Dharma body and wisdom life — they are the greatest obstacles to cultivating the Way.

To practice the Buddha's Dharma is simply this: do no evil; do all good.

See through it, and you are clear and bright; let go of it, and you are liberated. Liberation is being at ease. When the self is not present (not here), thieves and robbers will invade, and you will be swayed by external states.

Only a cultivator with no money at all can truly cultivate. Once there is money, cultivation becomes absolutely impossible. Of this I can assure you.

True happiness seeks nothing. When you reach the point of seeking nothing, you will have no worries. When you seek nothing at all, that is genuine joy — and it is also the true peace and stability of your own nature.

The worst bad habit of living beings is the mind of infatuated love and craving. Day and night they dwell in the midst of infatuation, never letting go for a single moment. If you could turn your lustful mind into a mind eager to learn Buddhism — never forgetting to study Buddhism for a single moment — you could become a Buddha very quickly.

Put your petty cleverness and intelligence aside. Do not think you know and understand everything. If you think there is nothing you do not know, then you are not someone who truly understands the Buddhadharma.

At the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas, no one is permitted to flatter or fawn, speaking sycophantic words to curry favor with others.

In a temple, at a Way-place, the worst thing of all is refusing to cultivate. Whoever does not cultivate will fall in the future.

Cultivation requires us to nurture simplicity — to act dull and simple-minded. The more naive and simple-minded, the better. Be so simple-minded that not even a single false thought remains.

Cultivators must not have a SELF. Throw the self into the garbage bin. Wherever you go, serve others and serve the public good. You must know how to blend your light with others (harmonize with everyone), taking yielding as your way forward. In all things, be cautious and restrained; never compete, scramble, or show off. Once you show off, trouble will find you at once.

(To monastics:) If the food and drink are not plain and simple, do not eat them. A cultivator's duty is to propagate the Dharma, not to wine and dine people. (This refers to monastics who frequent restaurants to entertain guests, or to discuss worldly affairs, fame and profit, and private matters.)

Some people live at the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas but will only come to listen to the lectures when the Master arrives; ordinarily they refuse to join the morning and evening recitation sessions. They hear the lectures yet refuse to rejoice along with others. That is truly selfish. They only want to come and take, not to come and give — the opposite of the basic spirit of the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas. The great assembly is one body; you cannot act in private selfishness, ignoring the assembly as a whole.

Who is the cultivator's enemy? It is not the demon king — it is selfishness. Working with a selfish mind, nothing will ever succeed; and even success would be mere illusion.

One who applies effort to cultivating the Way cannot let false thoughts arise for even a split second. As it is said: while the great matter is unfinished, grieve as if bereaved. While the great matter of birth and death is still unresolved, you should feel sorrowful, just like a child whose parents have newly died.

The Buddhadharma is as vast as the great sea: only with courageous vigor and diligent cultivation can you succeed.

Cultivators of the Way must have right understanding and right views. Do not confuse right and wrong. Black and white must be clearly distinguished; you cannot mistake a fish eye for a pearl. You cannot be sloppy and perfunctory. If you are, your understanding and views will be deviant (wrong knowledge and wrong views), and you will never become a Buddha.

Idle thinking: if you know for certain that something cannot be done, why do you deliberately keep thinking about it? If you know it is a false thought, idle thinking, why don't you set it aside? This is the bad habit of many people: knowing it is wrong, yet deliberately doing it. To put it bluntly, you have not seen through it and you have not let go (you are attached). If you are not attached here, you are attached there; if not attached to this thing, then attached to that; if not attached to men, then attached to women. And so you waste all your precious time.

Compassion springs from your own nature. It needs no contrivance to exist. You do not need to flatter (in order to have compassion); flattery is false. As people gradually mature, they will surely come to understand this truth. Then compassion will naturally arise in their hearts, without any need to deliberately do anything. Deliberately putting on a show of compassion, you will fall into softness and sycophancy. Deliberately putting on a show of non-compassion, you will become cold and distant. Going too far is no different from not going far enough. In all things you must hold to the Middle Way — that is, no mind, no thought.

As disciples of the Buddha, we must be careful about cause and effect. Do not casually slander or scold others.

When not a single thought arises, no ghost of any kind exists. When there is nothing left (no more greed, anger, delusion, false thoughts, or afflictions), then at that moment everything exists: the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas all come. Why? Because it is when you have nothing at all that the Buddhas come. If you still have a single thing (affliction, attachment), the Buddhas will not come. When you reach the realm of emptiness, you must exhaust your own habit-nature (afflictions and attachments) to its end, and reach the very end of the principle of human beings, the principle of the myriad things, the principle of heaven and earth. The Buddhas are you, and you are the Buddhas. When attachment to the four marks is all gone, what is left to afflict you?

If you understand (are enlightened), then everything is the patriarchs' intent. If you do not understand, then everything makes you upset and angry.

One wholesome thought, and heaven and earth are auspicious. One evil thought, and heaven and earth rage with storms. Therefore in any country whose people are good — who keep the five precepts and practice the ten good deeds — nothing (calamitous) will happen in that land.

If there are people who genuinely cultivate, Buddhism will flourish. If there are none, Buddhism will perish.

In cultivation, do not fear hardship, do not fear suffering, do not fear having no money, and do not fear having no food. If you harbor fear, you cannot cultivate. Cultivators of the Way are the opposite of worldly people: worldly people crave the five desires (money, sex, fame, food, and sleep for pleasure), and can never let go of them.

If you can endure without giving rise to desire (patiently refrain from stirring desires): that is keeping the precepts. If you cannot endure desire, that is not keeping the precepts.

In the life of the monastery, keeping the rules comes first. Attending the hall for the daily recitations, bowing, and the noon meal offering are duties you must perform. This is more important than anything else. You must follow the assembly (do as everyone does); you may not set yourself apart from the assembly (act differently from everyone). Otherwise you may not dwell together with the assembly.

If, in cultivation, you do not understand the Way, then you cultivate on one hand while leaking it away on the other (losing merit and virtue). For example, you are told not to give rise to lust, yet you give rise to even more lust. From morning to night you think of loving this one, craving that one. All impure thoughts. In your mind the water of wisdom will turn murky, and you will have no wisdom left, because the filth has been stirred up. Just because you do not understand the Way, you cultivate forever without realizing the fruit, without seeing the Way. Why? Because you harbor lustful desire. Without lustful desire, you would see the Way very quickly.

When you apply no effort and do not cultivate, you are like a whetstone for sharpening knives. You cannot see the stone wearing away, but after many days you will find that the stone has grown smaller and smaller.

Ignorance is a dark room. With wisdom, the dark room turns bright. In this world, the words MONEY and SC (sensual beauty) have ruined countless cultivators of the Way. If cultivators cannot let go of money, they will crave wealth and property; if they cannot let go of beauty, they will lust and crave sex. Their work in the Way can never succeed.

If your essence is full, you will not feel cold; if your vital energy is full, you will not feel hungry; if your spirit is full, you will not feel sleepy. Essence, energy, and spirit (in Taoism) are called the Three Treasures. This principle is similar to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha of Buddhism.

Miss by a hair's breadth, and you stray a thousand miles. In cultivating the Way you must not be sloppy or casual. If you give rise to false thoughts, fail to follow the monastic code, and are not earnest in learning the Way, you may instantly attract extremely severe retribution or punishment.

Leaving home is for the sake of cultivating pure conduct. If, after leaving home, you no longer wish to transcend the world — socializing, entertaining, and banqueting wherever you go — how can you be called a monastic?

Do not cling so tightly, carrying your burdens on your back forever. What burdens? Your bad habits and faults. If you keep such clutter, you will never pull your feet out of the mud, and you will never reach the other shore.

True cultivators of the Way, wherever they go, never hope for fine offerings of food or good lodgings. We should never harbor such thoughts, for they are the seeds of our downfall. Wherever you go, ordinary things are enough; never crave enjoyment. Do not be delighted with those who treat you well, and displeased with those who treat you badly.

Whoever does not flare up in anger will accord with the principles the Buddha taught, and will become a Buddha very easily.

People all abandon the root and chase the branches: they rank cultivation second, and rank making money first — forgetting the basic Way of being human, applying effort only to the branches. Working to earn money only sustains one's livelihood. Studying the Buddhadharma nourishes the Dharma body and wisdom life, increasing your wisdom. You should choose the sutra most suited to you and study it, instead of devoting yourself day after day solely to making money.

In learning to hold mantras, first of all the mind must be upright and the heart sincere. If the mind is not upright, whatever mantra you learn will turn deviant. Only with an upright mind will learning mantras bring response.

Within the bright light of your own nature, there is not a trace of greed. And within spiritual resonance, within wisdom, there is not the slightest bit of greed either. Therefore when greed arises in you, it is like a layer of dust suddenly appearing on a mirror. So we who apply effort in cultivation must always remember: do not be greedy for much, do not be greedy for speed, do not be greedy for bargains and comfort.

If there is a ghost in your mind, then you will fear ghosts. If there is no ghost in your mind, then ghosts will fear you.

Now that we have obtained a human body, if we do not use it to cultivate, when are we waiting for? Waiting until this body is lost — by then, wanting to cultivate will be too late.

Do not seek far away; you need not search for some lofty, profound Dharma door. When you hear the line The unsurpassed, deep, profound, subtle, wonderful Dharma, you think you must find some unsurpassed, subtle, wonderful Dharma. In truth, the lofty, profound, unsurpassed Dharma is too far from you, while you have not even taken the first step. Why abandon what is near and chase what is distant? Why abandon the root and follow the branches? Why not apply effort in cultivation right where you are — close to your own body, in your daily life? Why keep chasing after something so remote and wondrous? The ancients said: the Way is right beside you, yet you seek it far away; the matter is easy, yet you insist on finding the hard way.

If you truly never lie, then when you call to heaven, heaven will answer; when you call to earth, earth will reply.

No contending, no greed, no seeking, no selfishness, no self-benefit, no lying: this is the most effective method of cultivation.

Once you break the precept against lust, you will very easily break the precept against killing, and just as easily break the precepts against stealing and lying. Therefore, breaking the precept against lust embraces within it the precepts against killing, stealing, and lying.

Why do you give rise to afflictions? Because your greed has not yet stopped. You have not yet let go. As the saying goes: everywhere thorns, everywhere walls. (Thorns stand for afflictions. With afflictions come obstructions, just like walking into walls.) When you no longer have the four marks (the four attachments to notions of self, others, living beings, and a life span), who is left to suffer? If the sufferer does not exist, where could afflictions come from?

Be a dragon-elephant (a great talent) in the Dharma; do not be a little mouse in the Way.

In the heavens there are eighty-four thousand stars; on a person there are eighty-four thousand hairs. Human beings and the world correspond to each other. The reason the world is destroyed is that people have ignorance. The air in heaven and earth and the air within each person also correspond, for these two kinds of air can never be separated. Each person's air has its source. When people keep wholesome thoughts, it aids the righteous energy of heaven and earth. When a person flares up in anger and gives rise to a single afflicted thought, it increases the turbid energy in the universe. If everyone acts out of greed, anger, and delusion, there will be a great many calamities in heaven and earth. One person is so, and many people are likewise. Wherever evil people gather, disasters and calamities are a little more numerous. Thus, the goodness or badness of places in the world cannot be separated from the state of each one of us.

Worldly joy is brief; ultimate bliss alone is eternal. Therefore we must cultivate the Way.

To study Buddhism, you must learn compassion, virtue, and how to forgive others. Never harbor a mind of comparison, of winning and losing; never argue and quarrel with others.

Reverence transforms a hard, stubborn nature into a gentle, yielding one. To bow to the Buddha is to bow to the Buddha within your own nature. To become a Buddha is to become the Buddha of your own nature.

The ancients said: the noble person can reform destiny. People of virtue, the true and upright, can change their own lives and jump out of the wheel of fate. Why do misfortune and calamity occur? Because in our minds there are evil, inauspicious thoughts. Once bad seeds are planted, naturally bad fruits will be reaped. If we correct our faults and do good, we will meet with good, and evil will be kept far away.

Why do people encounter demonic karma? Because in the past they refused to listen to the guidance of good spiritual teachers, refused to accept their instruction. They gave free rein to false thoughts and created all manner of evil karma. So now they constantly suffer demonic harassment and entanglement. Nothing they do turns out as they wish.

I would like to ask a great favor of you: please give to me as alms your anger, as well as your ignorance, delusion, afflictions, and irritation.

The City of Ten Thousand Buddhas is the city of great compassion, the city of the Shurangama, the city of ten thousand Buddhas, the adamantine city, the city of the thousand hands and eyes, the city where the Proper Dharma long abides, the jeweled city. It is also the city for those who wish to cultivate, to seek blessings and wisdom — the place where the Buddhas of the ten directions gather.

When applying effort in cultivation, if you can endure and bear with fatigue no matter how tired you are, that is a kind of sincerity.

In cultivation, you must not waste the donors' money; you must economize with all your strength. If you waste material things and crave enjoyment, you will never succeed — because you refuse to cultivate blessings and wisdom.

What is wisdom? It is selflessness. What are false thoughts? They are precisely selfishness. Where there is selfishness, false thoughts will arise.

What am I, within empty space pervading the Dharma Realm? Fundamentally it has no past or present, no above or below, no self, no others, no living beings, no life span. Human beings originally manifest from within the great treasury of bright light.

To make Buddhism radiant, we must look far and wide. We must propagate Buddhism to every nation, every village, even to every mote of dust. There we will turn the great Dharma wheel and teach living beings, so that every being may leave suffering behind, gain joy, and escape the wheel of birth and death.

What is cultivation? It is cultivating until false thoughts are gone. Until desires are gone. That is precisely the skill.

Why do people have worries, sorrow, or fear? Because they still harbor emotional love and desire. When love and desire are cut off, there will be no more worry, sorrow, or fear.

What meaning is there, really, in men and women loving each other? However beautiful a face may be, it is only skin wrapping rot: inside there is excrement, urine... The nine openings of the body constantly ooze impurities: the eyes have eye-gum, the ears have earwax, the nose has mucus, the mouth has saliva, plus urine and excrement. Do you think this body is ultimately clean?

If you do not cultivate, then even if Shakyamuni Buddha himself were your teacher, it would be of no benefit.

When you recite Guanyin Bodhisattva's name, do not look at everyone and see only their faults. If you specialize in finding what's wrong with others, your own suffering has not yet been removed. The root of suffering has not been cut off.

Craving for money drives people mad. Craving for sex also drives people mad. Craving for fame leaves them reeling. Craving for food makes them even more upside-down. And craving for sleep and pleasure sends them spinning. Money, beauty, fame, food, and sleep for pleasure are the five roots of hell. Yet every one of us buries these roots deep in our hearts. Wholesome roots we fail to plant deeply, while we plant the five desires deeper and deeper. Ah! Thinking they are still not deep enough, we keep burying them deeper still!

Why will the world one day be destroyed? Because in people, wholesome thoughts are few and evil thoughts are many. With one good thought, heaven and earth gain righteous energy. With one evil thought, heaven and earth gain more poisonous energy. We must turn bad energy into wholesome energy.

In cultivation, morality must be present everywhere. Taking non-obstruction of morality as the root of keeping the precepts.

All those who treat you without compassion, or who do not speak to you decently, are your good spiritual teachers. If you meet adversity yet can endure it — meeting extremely disagreeable, unpleasant things yet still handling them with composure — then your skill in patience can be seen. Do not let a single sentence shake your mind. If you cultivate to the point of being unmoved, able to endure what others cannot endure, that is genuine skill. If you cannot yet do this, you must start over from the beginning.

Cultivators of the Way should be like water — always humble and lowly, never vying for merit, never craving virtue. Give all good things to others; take all bad things upon yourself.

Why are people born as humans? Because of emotional love (craving), they are reborn into this world of the five turbidities. If that emotional love were lessened, we could be born elsewhere — in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, the Lapis Lazuli Land, or other worlds. The ancients said: "If love is not heavy, one is not born in the Saha world; if karma is not ended, one is not born in the Pure Land."

Vigor means vigor of body and vigor of mind. Vigor of body means reciting sutras, bowing, sitting in meditation, and holding mantras — using the body to cultivate. Vigor of mind means that in every place and at every moment you diligently cultivate morality, samadhi, and wisdom, and put an end to greed, anger, and delusion. Vigorous by day and vigorous by night, always pressing forward, never lazy. For cultivators, vigor is supremely important. We cannot do without vigor, for without vigor we cannot become Buddhas. To become a Buddha, you must be vigorous.

Each person's body is a hell — only we do not know it.

Guanyin Bodhisattva looks within, while we look outward. Guanyin Bodhisattva looks into her own nature; her own nature and that of every living being are as if joined by electric wires: whatever false thought a being stirs, she knows it all.

One who keeps the precepts purifies his own nature: sweeping clean all the dark, ugly things within his own nature.

In applying effort, do not fear suffering, hardship, or fatigue — only then can you succeed.

Who is the mother that gave birth to the atomic bomb, the hydrogen bomb, and the laser? It is none other than greed, anger, and delusion. Therefore, if we wipe out greed, anger, and delusion, the atomic bomb will not explode, the hydrogen bomb will not detonate, and the laser will be of no more use.

In cultivation you must keep a balanced state day after day, like a weighing scale. How to stay balanced? At all times keep a calm, still attitude, without a single ripple stirring in your own nature. This is precisely "affliction is enlightenment; birth and death are nirvana."

Cultivators of the Way cultivate less and less, decreasing until nothing at all remains. Do not follow the ways of worldly people, who want more of everything.

To end birth and death, you must hang the two words "birth and death" upon your eyebrows. Opening your eyes, you see the question of birth and death; closing your eyes, you see the question of birth and death. Only by applying effort in cultivation at all times and in all places can you cut off birth and death.

The first thing Buddhist learners must do is get rid of their temper. If the temper does not stop, then however much Buddhadharma you study, you are only planting the cause of an asura — and your future reward will be rebirth as an asura.

Cultivators must not, upon seeing others, put on a blank, indifferent face and ignore them. That is impolite. Monastics and laypeople alike must be courteous in dealing with others. Lacking courtesy means lacking culture. We must be refined in both substance and expression (elegant, gentle, and polite in character), never crude or wild.

If you give rise to not even a single false thought for an instant, making the mind pure, then after a long time your mind will become still and ever quiet.

Virtue and morality are like the sun and moon, like heaven and earth. They are also a person's very life. Without virtue, a person is like one with no life, with no sun, moon, heaven, or earth.

Whether Chan meditation or Buddha recitation, both are good. Only be genuine in cultivation, and you can pass through the gate of birth and death. At life's end there will be no pain, no craving in the heart; like entering samadhi, you will smile and be reborn (in the Pure Land).

Cultivators of the Way must do deeds of non-action: that is, accumulate merit and virtue without ever clinging to them.

When you take refuge in the Triple Jewel — the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha — you must also take refuge in the precepts. After taking refuge, you must deeply believe in the Triple Jewel. Within the scope of the Buddha's teaching, you must do meaningful things. Do not believe in the Buddhadharma out of greed.

In studying the Buddhadharma, the essential thing is to have the eye that discerns the truth (the Dharma-discerning eye). If you just believe this story and that story (without observing to see the true face of the matter), you will accomplish nothing in the end.

Purity means not craving money and having no need of sex either.

When someone teaches you a Dharma for getting rich, observe: has he himself gotten rich? If he has money, it is surely because you gave it to him — because you wanted to learn the money-making Dharma. Just like buying stocks: you must buy so many shares before you can hope for profit. You have to pay, to make offerings to that man first — perhaps a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred thousand — so that through this he becomes flush with money. Then he talks about emitting red light, yellow light, black light, purple light...? It is all a fraud. Precisely because I do not know how to transmit any money-making Dharma, I must loudly expose this Dharma's secret.

Natural disasters are not really calamities of heaven, for heaven has no calamities — it is we humans who suffer them. Man-made calamities are what we do to ourselves and must ourselves bear.

In cultivation, do not go seeking the Way on South Mountain, in the North Sea, in the Western Heaven, or in the Eastern Land. The Way is right in your own body, so do not seek outwardly. Yet people always love to search in distant, lofty places.

People's temperament is very selfish. Knowing something is wrong, if it benefits them they still charge ahead and do it. Hence:

Khuyến quân vi thiện, viết vô tiền: hữu dã vô.

Họa đáo lâm đầu, dụng vạn thiên: vô dã hữu.

Nhược yếu dữ quân đàm thiện sự: khứ dã mang.

Nhất triều mệnh tận, tán hoàng tuyền: mang dã khứ.

Which means:

I urge you to do good, (and you say:) "I have no money" — even with money, you say you have none.

When calamity lands on your head and you must spend thousands upon thousands: with no money, you still must find some.

If I wish to discuss good deeds with you: you are too busy even to go.

One day when life ends and you sink to the Yellow Springs: busy or not, you still must go.

Buddhist learners should first learn to accept loss and never crave advantage. In all things you must know how to let go. Only by letting go can you attain realization.

All dharmas are the Buddhadharma, and none can be grasped. Yet we can also say that all dharmas are not the Buddhadharma. In short: in studying Buddhism, we must let go of all attachments. Sweep away all dharmas; leave behind all marks. Whatever has marks is all false and cannot be grasped. If you see all marks as markless, then you see the Tathagata.





The greatest taboo for Buddhist learners is attachment. Before studying Buddhism there were not many attachments; after studying Buddhism there are even more! In truth, all things at all times proclaim the truth. If you are enlightened, you will naturally see through everything. If you are not enlightened, the more attached you are, the deeper you sink, the more deluded you become.

Every Buddhist follower must shoulder the responsibility of making Buddhism flourish.

The strongest karmic force in the world is the karma of killing. The retribution for killing outweighs all other karma. Living beings slaughter one another in turn, taking revenge on one another — truly the most tragic affair in this world.

Cultivators must train in the skill of patience: endure cold, endure heat, endure wind, endure rain; endure hunger, endure thirst; endure scolding, endure beating. We should learn the spirit of Never Disparaging Bodhisattva: no matter who treats me badly, I will not give rise to anger; I will only treat them with sincerity, until they are naturally moved and transformed, turning weapons into silk.

Why must we cultivate? Because we are deluded, doing only upside-down things, suffering in the wheel of rebirth, never free.

A person's lot in life comes from karmic force. We should not let our inborn nature and habits lead us by the nose, nor let desires and material things delude us. We must create our own destiny and steer our own fate. To change your destiny, do a great many meritorious and virtuous deeds. Then, when calamity meets you, good will naturally arrive. Evil will turn into auspiciousness. As the saying goes: just do good deeds; do not ask what results the future will bring.

Everyone knows that patience carries you to the shore of liberation. But when states come (things against your wishes), you cannot bear them. The fire of ignorance, three feet high, in a single instant burns clean all the merit and virtue accumulated over many long years.

To contemplate with freedom and ease is to be a Bodhisattva. To contemplate without freedom and ease is to be an ordinary person.

Treat everyone well: deal with them with kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity. Toward everyone you must have compassion. Even if someone is the worst villain, you must still show compassion, in order to move and transform them. If you cannot transform them this time, wait and transform them next time. If you cannot transform them in this life, vow that in the next life you will surely transform them, making them reform from evil and do good. In the Flower Adornment Sutra, a Bodhisattva, in order to save a single being, follows that being for ever so many great eons. No matter the hardship and suffering, no matter the adversity, he never retreats — single-mindedly wishing only to move and transform that being.

To become a Buddha you must cut off desires, sever emotional love; with a pure mind and few desires, only then can great wisdom open.

What is cultivation? It is cultivating the mind. What must the mind be like? It must be single-minded. As it is said: attain the M"T (singleness of mind), and all matters are done. You must concentrate your will in cultivation. Once your thoughts are concentrated, wisdom will open. With unconcentrated thoughts, the mind will chase after externals.

Cultivators of the Way must not flare up. Whoever has no temper is one with the Way, one with the Dharma. When you do not flare up, hatred has no place; when hatred is gone, delusion is gone too. Why are we deluded? Because our hatred is too great. Once anger flares, we fear nothing: neither heaven nor earth. Then we refute the principle of cause and effect, turn black and white upside down, and do things that accord with neither the precepts, nor the law, nor human decency and reason.

We Buddhist learners must first diligently cultivate morality, samadhi, and wisdom, and wipe out greed, anger, and delusion. This is something each person must personally practice and apply to this very body, truly applying effort. It is not a matter of telling others to diligently cultivate morality, samadhi, and wisdom and wipe out greed, anger, and delusion — you must yourself truly cultivate.

Do not harbor wild ambitions, savage schemes, and so many deluded false thoughts. Thinking wildly does nothing to help your cultivation.

To see through your own delusion, you must know how to turn the hearing around to listen to your own nature.

In cultivation you must be kind in heart and humble in spirit. Kind in heart means being kindly and compassionate to everyone. Humble in spirit means having no arrogance, and no attachment to the four marks. Only by smashing all such attachments can you walk the Bodhisattva path.

Read the Sutra of Not Getting Angry, read the Sutra of Not Scolding, read the Sutra of No Hatred. Once you have read these three sutras, you will become a Buddha very quickly.

True cultivators of the Way: their every move and act is self-restrained; walking, standing, sitting, and lying never leave home. Do not be a mirror that only reflects other people's images (appearing on the mirror) without ever reflecting itself.

Those who practice meditation must practice it in every place and at every moment. That is, they must gather in body and mind, never indulgent, never scattered.

Monastics are good models for laypeople. If you are not a good model, laypeople will not have faith. Then your influence will be gone. Therefore monastics must be good models for laypeople.

We cultivators should eat plain, tasteless food. Only then can we smash attachments and get rid of our bad habits.

If you do not waste your essence, energy, and spirit, then whether you eat or not is no longer an issue. It is precisely because day after day we keep revolving in tainted states that we need to eat and drink.

You should deeply enter and practice a single Dharma door: meditators must concentrate wholeheartedly on Chan; scholars of doctrine must concentrate wholeheartedly on the Teachings school; Vinaya students must specialize in the Vinaya school; mantra holders must concentrate on the Esoteric school; Buddha reciters must single-mindedly recite the Buddha's name. When you recite to singlemindedness without confusion, you will surely be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Do not study Chan while also wanting to study doctrine, Vinaya, Esotericism, and the Pure Land. When you crave many dishes, you cannot chew any of them well. You must be single-minded and dedicated in applying effort; only then will you succeed. It is like having only one mouth: with your mouth stuffed full of food, you cannot chew it fine. Too full a mouth, and you cannot even swallow your rice. Studying Buddhism is the same: step by step, in order, slowly advancing. Do not crave speed. As the saying goes: "Haste makes waste — wanting speed, you never arrive."

What is true patience? Toward those who are not your equals — whose position is lower than yours, whose wisdom is less than yours, whose learning falls short — inferior to you in everything: when they treat you rudely and unkindly and you can still be patient, that is true patience. This patience is not patience toward those above you in rank. Toward those above you, you are merely submitting — that is not patience.

Flaring up is evil. Not flaring up is good.

Buddhist learners should not look outward: running east, west, north, and south, wandering everywhere, wasting all their time.

Why do people get sick? Because in ordinary times they pay no attention to health. Laypeople should cut down on lustful conduct and increase physical exercise. That is the root of health. If you indulge in sex all day without restraint or rule, your body can never be healthy.

When things develop to the extreme, they reverse; when blockage reaches the extreme, it opens into flow - when a matter develops to its peak, it will turn in the opposite direction; when stuck to the extreme, it will become unblocked. Opposition is the movement of the Way; softness is the function of the Way - only with opposition is there movement (of the Way); the usefulness (of the Way) lies in softness. If you can look at the reverse side of every matter and find what is good and wholesome in it, then all will be fine and nothing will be troublesome.

When eating, whether the food is well-cooked or undercooked, tasty or bland, do not cling to its flavors.

Cultivators of the Way must know how to economize and cherish blessings everywhere, and must not waste money and goods. Doing so over days and months will accumulate virtue for yourself. From such seeds of thrift, leafy trees will grow and fruit will abound. Without fertilizer and watering, leaves easily wither and die. Therefore cultivators of the Way must value virtue — the foremost fundamental precept.

In this world, those who want what is false throw away what is true. If you want to find what is true, you must let go of what is false. You cannot cultivate a world-transcending Dharma without letting go of worldly dharmas.

The Buddhadharma is the religion that proclaims selflessness. It does not approve of physiognomy, astrology, divination, much less belief in feng shui. For these things run counter to the Buddhadharma, counter to the Way. That is why their spread is forbidden within the Way. When you believe in such things, a self remains. From that self, everything arises; for that self, everything is calculated. Having a self and no others is a principle incompatible with the Buddhadharma.

The Dharma I teach is very simple and plain. What Dharma? The Dharma of eating, wearing clothes, and sleeping. So when people come seeking the Dharma, I teach them to eat a little less, wear a little less, sleep a little less. For: wearing less increases blessings, eating less increases longevity, sleeping less increases prosperity. When these three stars (blessing, prosperity, longevity) all shine upon you — is that not the Buddhadharma too?

If there is no fire in the liver (no anger arising)

Every illness can be avoided.

This is a wonderful medicine,

Yet it is shelved in a corner (no one will use it).

Ta bà ha!

What does attachment mean? When you do not believe in cause and effect, deep attachment will arise. Such attachment leads to slander — claiming there is no principle of cause and effect. Therefore Buddhists must clearly recognize the principle of cause and effect. Why must we deeply believe in cause and effect? Without believing in cause and effect, you can hardly be a Buddhist. Without reading and reciting the Mahayana sutras, wisdom will not open.

What are false thoughts? They are desires overflowing the brim.

Diligent precept-keeping must be practiced where no one can see. It is not diligence in front of others, keeping precepts in front of people. It must be when you are all alone by yourself that you diligently keep the precepts.

Cultivating today, you think you'll become a Buddha tomorrow! Just hoeing the ground, you think you've finished digging the well! There is no such thing! Cultivation is like grinding iron into a needle: when the effort is complete, realization comes naturally.

I am changing the words "Buddhism" into "Mind-ism," for everyone has a mind. Cultivation means casting out the false mind and keeping the true mind. With a false mind you remain an ordinary person; with a true mind you are a Buddha.

When Chan practice ripens, not only will false thoughts vanish, but the temper will also dissolve, afflictions lessen, character soar, and bearing grow all the greater.

The principle of Buddhism is that everyone can become a Buddha. The living beings of the present are our parents of the past, and also the Buddhas of the future. If we give rise to hatred toward living beings, it is hatred toward our parents and toward the Buddhas — and we become utterly unfilial.

When we are amid calamities, epidemics, and turmoil, we should genuinely and sincerely apply effort in cultivation — only then can bad energy turn auspicious, and disasters turn to peace.

While within birth and death, if you want to escape birth and death you must spend some strength. Escaping birth and death is not easy. What does spending strength mean? It means that whatever you do, you truly do it. Meeting adversity — the harder and more trying it is — the more unmoved you are, the less you flare up in anger. That is tending the plot of earth in your mind, nourishing the sky of your own nature. Doing so, you add righteous energy to heaven and earth. Only then are you a true cultivator of the Way, one who truly believes in the Buddha.

To see through is to understand completely; to let go is to be liberated. With liberation, you are free and at ease. Without liberation, you cannot be at ease. To be not at ease with oneself is just this.

Cultivation is nothing else: right here in this body, mind, and life, apply the skill.

This Dharma removes greed, anger, and delusion, and cultivates morality, samadhi, and wisdom. If you go looking for something mysterious, you only go against the Way. This Way is: the ordinary mind is the Way; the upright mind is the Way-place.

Cultivators must remember: never form defiled, entangled affinities with others. For that breeds entanglement and bondage, a tangled mess, and in the end it will make you fall.

I only beg for great alms, not for small alms (begging for alms means going out to ask). What is begging for great alms? It means I want to beg for your ignorance, your anger, your afflictions. When you no longer have these three — ignorance, anger, affliction — you will enjoy auspiciousness as you wish. With these three, there are evil spirits and evil affairs. So, friends! Let go of what you cannot let go of; what you can throw away, throw away at once! Throw away ignorance, anger, and affliction, and all will be well with you.

The chief purpose of cultivation is to end birth and death — not to seek spiritual responses.

Chan meditators must recognize the basic issue. What is it? Bad habits and faults. When we "hit the seven" (a Chan retreat week), it means hitting (striking down) bad habits and faults.

Whatever the matter, if you regard it as quite ordinary, nothing very important, then there will be no trouble. When you take this or that affair as weighty, as terribly important, then it becomes troublesome.

In cultivating the Way, cultivate genuine virtue and morality: never obstruct others, and never fear others obstructing you.

The hardest thing in cultivation is severing afflictions. To sever means to transform — transforming afflictions into enlightenment (bodhi).

Think lightly of wealth, sex, fame, food, and sleep; treat them as nothing; forget them — only then are you truly a cultivator.

The Land of Ultimate Bliss is manifested by the mind. Our own nature is the Pure Land; our own nature is Amitabha Buddha. When there are no false thoughts, that mind is the Pure Land. When there are no afflictions, that mind is Amitabha.

The Way is precious in a concentrated mind. Just as in warfare, what counts is well-trained troops, not numbers. None of your actions should stray from your own nature. When in the assembly, guard your speech and beware the six thieves (ear, eye, nose, tongue, body, mind). Never let the six thieves drag you away.

Believing in the Buddha, we must not be divisive — deeming (our own religion) supreme, ourselves right (and others wrong), ourselves so fine and special. With even one such thought, you are unfit to build anything. Every child of the Buddha should have a broad, all-embracing heart that enfolds all beings. Within the scope of Buddhism, we have no enemies.

When reciting Guanyin Bodhisattva's name, we (the few cultivators dwelling in the temple) should not day and night keep stirring false thoughts, thinking: "This morning there was nothing to eat, tonight there is not even tea to drink — such suffering, unbearable! I must run away!"

Without patience, no Dharma can be cultivated to success. Without patience, you will always feel this is wrong, that is no good. Everything goes against your wishes. Then what can you cultivate? In the Way there is no view of self, and no clinging to self either.

Cultivators must cultivate the mark of selflessness. Without the mark of self, you can endure all things; whatever states come, your mind is unmoved, for you regard yourself as empty space. When favorable states come, cultivate; when adverse states come, also cultivate. When favorable states arrive, give rise to no delight; when adverse states arrive, give rise to no sorrow. Adverse or favorable, you must see them clearly. If you can remain thus unmoved, no state can shake you. If you are constantly clear and bright, only then can you turn states around.

A cultivator who does not wear the sash is no different from one who has returned to lay life — just like an ordinary worldly person. Nor does wearing the long robe prove that you are a monastic. Even wearing the sash, if day after day you break the precepts and never truly cultivate, you do not deserve to be called a monastic — how much less if you do not even wear the sash, lacking the very appearance of a bhikshu.

Demons are things that help us cultivate the Way. Demons help us from the reverse side, testing whether our vows are firm. If you are truly firm, then even a thousand demons cannot move you, and ten thousand demons cannot make you retreat. You fear nothing, because you seek nothing.

To nurture energy, do not talk too much. Cultivators who do not know how to speak little cannot cultivate. Without nourishing your energy, there is no Dharma. Talking on and on, the Dharma all leaks away. Then what Way can you still cultivate?

In truth, all things proclaim the Dharma. The table speaks the table's Dharma. The chair speaks the chair's Dharma. Every affair, every matter turns the Dharma wheel. People turn the Dharma wheel of people. Cats turn the Dharma wheel of cats. If you understand clearly, you will hear the Dharma of clear understanding. If you do not understand, you will only hear the Dharma of delusion.

Do not let fame and profit delude your mind. At death, your hands are still empty. As the saying goes: Do not wait until old to study the Way; the graveyards are full of the young.

The bad habit of Buddhist followers is that everyone thinks they are right, caring nothing for others; no one admits their own mistakes, while instead they ostracize one another and speak ill of one another.

In the course of cultivation there is never a moment for laziness. In cultivating the Way you must persist unceasingly, never letting it break. Otherwise, cultivating for eons as countless as the Ganges' sands is like cooking sand and hoping for rice. That can never be.

With genuine, unobstructed eloquence, there is no need for polished words. For such words come forth from the bright light of one's own nature, from the Tathagata's treasury of wisdom. Using choice, polished words has the opposite effect, turning good into bad. The ancients said:

Cleverness comes from doing hidden good. (Hidden good means good deeds done in silence, unknown to others)

Hidden good leads onto the road of cleverness.

Without doing hidden good to gain cleverness,

Cleverness will be cheated by cleverness.

Love your body: do not let it break the law.

Love your family: do not let it fall apart.

Love your country: sacrifice yourself for the nation.

It is not the case that eating vegetarian food means keeping the precept against killing. Nor should you say, "I have never personally killed any being," and conclude you have not broken the precept against killing. The precept against killing requires that in your mind you give rise to no hatred toward living beings.

When you harbor fear, then even if you do not want demons to come, demons will come. If you have no fearful mind, then even if demons wish to come, they cannot come. This is the most important secret: have no fear. When you are fearless, your mind will be upright. Uprightness can subdue all things, for the deviant never overcomes the upright. That is why demons fear most the four words: upright, great, bright, and open.

One who has illumined the mind is not deluded. One who has seen the nature does not grieve. The mind is like a bright mirror, and also like still water.

You should: follow conditions to dissolve old karma, and create no new offenses.

The self-satisfied (arrogant, deeming themselves too good, too capable, too complete) can never accomplish anything. We must learn: having, yet as if having not; true, yet as if false. With lofty virtue and morality, appear as if possessing nothing at all. One who truly has talent looks as if having no talent at all.

Here are six "don'ts":

When sitting, don't swing your legs or shake your knees.

When standing, don't shake your clothes.

When walking, don't look back.

When speaking, don't stick out your tongue.

When laughing, don't laugh loudly.

When angry, don't shout and yell.

Train yourself: think carefully before speaking, be happy within before laughing, and act only when the deed is meaningful.

All conditioned dharmas in this world are truly fragile, with nothing certain about them. Nothing lasts forever without changing. No thing, no matter, is solid.

Those of us who constantly flare up in anger, igniting the fire of ignorance, are caught in the demons' net. How to escape the demons' net? Very easy: do not get angry. Without flaring up, without the fire of ignorance, without hatred, you escape the demons' net at once.

Our body is false — so why do we keep clinging to it? Why keep creating offenses for its sake, unable to let go?

Cultivators of the Way must practice distancing: distance yourself from wealth, sex, fame, food, and sleep; distance yourself from all evil. Draw near to all good.

Whoever can subdue the six senses, the six objects, and the six consciousnesses, making them obey and not rebel — such a one is a Bodhisattva.

Whoever can sweep emotions clean, with no more garbage and filth in the heart — such a one is a Bodhisattva.

Awaken! Realize that human life is impermanent. The Ghost of Impermanence — no one knows when it will come for you. Then: a thousand things you cannot bring along; only karma follows you. If you do not apply effort now, when will you cultivate, in which eon?

You should know that the two words fame and profit harm all worldly people.

Without greedy desire, no affliction of any kind exists. Once greedy desire exists, everything happens. The world, the myriad things and myriad beings — everything is born from greedy desire.

In truth, mountain goblins, water monsters, spirits, and the like are no idle talk. But looking at it the other way: if you keep your mind pure, with no deviant thoughts, then at all times heavenly dragons will protect you. Hold your mind firm and leave no gaps, and from where could demonic obstacles enter?

Those with wisdom have no afflictions.

The false stands upon the true. When the false is ended, the true appears. While the false is unended, the true does not appear.

Buddhist learners, upon hearing praise, should not get so pleased and elated; hearing a single disagreeable sentence, they become immensely afflicted. That shows a lack of samadhi power. With samadhi power, you will not be swayed by the states of the eight winds.

At all times you must cultivate; at all times diligently seek escape from this dusty world.

Birth and death are so perilous, yet you still dare to be lazy! You even put on an air as if nothing were the matter, as though your samadhi power were great. Is that not wasting time?

Virtuous eminent monks of old usually came invisibly and left without a trace. Coming, they drifted like clouds; going, they vanished in a flash. Coming like a passing breeze, going like a passing breeze. (Though their virtuous influence flows on for all ages.) Coming with no hindrance, going with no hindrance.

Diligently cultivating morality, samadhi, and wisdom means the noble person presses forward. When greed, anger, and delusion are wiped out, we need no longer head downward.

Demons are extremely clever. Spying out what someone craves, they use the fitting method to lure that person. Therefore we cultivators need not recite any special mantra, nor use any special Dharma door. Only be genuine — no contending, no greed, no seeking, no selfishness, no self-benefit — and diligently endure hardship in cultivation; then no demon can harm you. But if you harbor greed, pride, the wish to take advantage, the wish to find a shortcut in cultivation, then you will easily fall into demonic events.

When a defiled thought is born, that is the Saha world.

When a pure thought is born, that is the Land of Ultimate Bliss. The Lapis Lazuli Land and Ultimate Bliss are in no way different.

Building temples is not as good as building people. Building people is not as good as building Buddhas.

You must decide on the spot (the moment things happen, decide what to do). Do not be wishy-washy, hesitating and indecisive, dragging on and on, losing precious opportunities. Do not shuffle your feet in indecision; quickly sever afflictions and end birth and death.

Heaven and earth cannot lack harmonious energy for a single day; the human heart cannot lack the god of joy (gladness) for a single day. Day after day invite the god of joy into your heart; befriend the god of joy. Then you will have no afflictions. This is very important for cultivators too.

We must quell the world's wars — not by opposing war. When you harbor an anti-war mind, war has already broken out within your own body. When you oppose others, or resist war, war has already arisen in your mind.

You do not believe in the retribution of cause and effect? Just wait until it lands on your head — then, try to dodge it if you can.

Sitting in full lotus makes it easy to enter samadhi. But if you can enter samadhi while walking, then sitting or not sitting is the same. The state of samadhi is utter silence of false thoughts: no thought arising in the mind, unstained by a speck of dust. If, while walking, standing, sitting, or lying, you give rise to no thought and are stained by no dust — that is where you apply effort. Sitting down is not the only thing called applying effort.

Do not let false marks drive you mad.

There must be no mistaking the principle of cause and effect, and no stalling in cultivation.

Cultivators stay far from fame and profit. They see wealth and honor as dewdrops among flowers. They see rank and renown as vapor on roof tiles, vanishing traceless in an instant. If you want to test whether someone cultivates, look at whether their deeds and actions aim at fame and profit.

Not crying, not laughing — that is called samadhi power. Without samadhi power, one cries and laughs all the time.

Constant vigor is itself dwelling in samadhi. If you can accord with outer conditions without changing — never altering your resolve, yet able to adapt to circumstances — that is called Vajra Samadhi. Vajra Samadhi has no form; it is simply the indestructible resolve for enlightenment (bodhicitta), nothing more.

If you can see through the seven emotions — joy, anger, sorrow, fear, love, hatred, and craving — you can subdue them. Do not let them raise waves and winds, and your mind is subdued.

The most urgent matter today is that the world is overrun with little ghosts, more than can be counted. Why so many little ghosts? Because people have too many abortions. Fetuses, not yet formed, are killed — and as ghosts they harbor extremely heavy vengeful hearts. Thus keeping the precept against killing, freeing captive creatures, and eating vegetarian all include not having abortions. These little ghosts are truly not easy to save and cross over. As the saying goes: King Yama is easy to meet; little ghosts are hard to cross over.

Those lacking in virtue have huge tempers, and deep, thick ignorance and delusion. Those with virtue have no temper at all, and ignorance has already been transformed into wisdom. That is why cultivators must foster virtue.

People constantly compare themselves, deeming themselves better than others. In truth, while body and mind have not yet reached the realm of emptiness, they are all attached to the mark of self. Chan meditators must get rid of the self. Not only must there be no mark or notion of self — there must be no mind, no body. When body and mind are both empty, you will be a Way-person of no mind.

When truly free of false thoughts, you will be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Without false thoughts there are no afflictions, no suffering. That is precisely the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Know to want little and be content (fewer desires, knowing you have enough). When you know you already have enough of everything, nothing will go wrong.

None of us should merely chant the Diamond Sutra, the Amitabha Sutra, the Dharma Flower Sutra, or the Shurangama Sutra with our lips. You must chant clearly the sutra within your own mind — only then is it good. To chant the true sutra means: the mind harbors no jealousy, no arrogance, no heavy clinging to self, no stubborn gripping of your own views. If you have these bad habits, then though you chant sutras, you do not know how to chant.

Those with a temper suffer. Those without a temper are at ease. The hot-tempered have afflictions; the even-tempered are usually cheerful. Temper is your greatest enemy. Why do people fall sick? Because of temper. Why does nothing go smoothly? Also because of temper. If at all times, in every moment, you never flare up in anger, then at all times you are joyful, carefree, and at peace.

To cultivate the Way you must nourish virtue and morality. Without virtuous conduct, cultivation is impossible.

Cultivating the Way requires you to be genuine and honest. It is like spinning thread: strand by strand must be drawn out, so that nothing tangles.

Do not look for scientific methods to reach enlightenment. Do not try to be clever.

On each person's body there are countless, boundless beings. If you harbor greed, those beings also harbor greed; if you harbor anger, each of those beings imitates you and flares up too. Your greed, anger, and delusion can influence those beings. The small ones multiply into a great many; the big ones grow bigger still. These are precisely your hundreds of thousands of millions of transformation bodies! Therefore cultivators of the Way must, with every movement of mind, reform bad habits and cultivate good ones.

The five skandhas are shackles binding people. Covered over by the four elements and the five skandhas, we cannot be liberated.

Without gentleness and humility, how can you save others? You probably cannot even save yourself.

Fellow cultivators and Dharma friends should encourage one another and walk the path of enlightenment together. Do not harm one another. At all times speak the Dharma for one another to hear. Let the mouth speak no improper words; let the body do no improper deeds.

Cultivation requires turning the light around and shining it within (gathering the light back to shine upon the mind). It is not a matter of shining light outward so that others notice you.

Cultivate without contending, and there will be no demons. Contend, and demons arrive at once.

In choosing friends, choose good friends, beneficial friends. Do not choose bad friends and do wicked things together, so that in the end both fall.

Before realization, your halo is still young. Such a halo is still faint and weak, unable to withstand wind, waves, and storms. Only when the halo is perfect — neither lacking nor excess — may it shine forth. At present you are in the stage of cultivation: do not shine your light.

As humans, you refuse to cultivate well. By the time you become oxen, sheep, pigs, or horses, you will have no more chance to cultivate. Then, kneeling at the butcher's door, you will weep and beg: "Please be merciful, spare my life!" But the butcher will kill you just the same. So whenever you hear the pitiful cries at the slaughterhouse, you will understand where calamities and wars come from.

In cultivation you should not speak carelessly. Otherwise you will suffer the retribution of being mute.

Earthquakes (the earth shaking) can be called human quakes (people shaking), for earth and people are connected. When people quake, the earth quakes. If people do not quake, the earth does not quake either. When you are gleeful, the earth quakes; when you flare up, the earth also quakes. Sorrow, worry, fear, love, and hatred all bring earthquakes. With lust and emotional desire, earthquakes grow greater still. Shaking within, the outside shakes too. Only with inner earthquakes are there outer earthquakes. They are linked. You plant the quake-causing seed within, and so outer earthquakes occur. When planting the seed you feel no fear; only when it ripens into fruit are you scared to death.

Cultivation requires diligence and the endurance of hardship.

The method of applying effort is to turn the light around and reflect within, thought after thought. It is not a matter of reciting some mantra — only that, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, you never leave home (your true mind, your resolve for enlightenment), never run outside chasing after things. Nor is it to be sought in books. Pay attention to emptiness. If you truly experience it, you will be greedy for nothing. For you yourself have always been complete. This emptiness is true emptiness. From within it, wonderful existence arises. Hence: doing no evil is (true emptiness); doing all good is (wonderful existence). The precepts are the model that cultivators rely on to practice. When you reach "emptiness," all karmic obstacles are empty too — neither offense nor blessing remains.

Demons come from all directions to test cultivators. If you apply effort while tangled in rights and wrongs, self and others, joy and sorrow, love and hatred, demons will take advantage and slip in through those very gaps.

To be born in Ultimate Bliss, you must gather in and sweep clean all emotions.

Why is there war in the world? When people began to eat meat, wars also began. Eating meat is eating people.

One who points out my faults is my teacher. Whoever can speak of your bad habits and faults is a good spiritual teacher. You should thank such a person; do not regard them as an enemy.

The deluded believe in feng shui; the wise believe in the feng shui of the mind. All is made by the mind.

Worldly people think learning is found in vast places (like mountains), never suspecting that learning lies right here in this tiny place (your own mind). If you have virtue, the feng shui is naturally good, because your mind is good.

The wise see straight through to the principle of matters, unblocked by outer appearances. The foolish see only the outward marks of matters, never seeing through to the truth within.

If you wish to know the Buddhas of the three periods of time, contemplate the nature of the Dharma Realm: everything is made by the mind alone.

To gain wisdom, first of all do not scold others, nor beat, kill, or harm them.

We must render service to the world and benefit others. If all you do is scheme for your own profit, caring only for your own comfort — what meaning is there in being human?

What do I know? I know what it means to accept loss and never take advantage. If you truly understand, you will know: accepting loss is gaining advantage (winning), while grabbing advantage (struggling to win) is suffering loss.

Small faults and bad habits are not easy to correct. If you can correct them, you will have samadhi power.

Worldly people deem getting rich the greatest joy. Once they have money, they rack their brains over how to guard it so it will not be lost or spent. Assuming money is truly theirs, they worry day after day. Yet whether much or little, at death not a penny can be taken along — and both hands are empty again! Tell me, what joy is there in that?

We are all led by karma, so that: the body is not its own master. We are born into this life to repay debts. Because the karma created in the past differs, the retribution borne in this life differs too. This is the net of karma, woven and knotted.

Doing the deeds of ghosts makes you a ghost. Doing the deeds of humans makes you human. Doing the deeds of Buddhas makes you a Buddha.

Now that you have heard the words "Great Compassion Mantra," you should rejoice, thinking how fortunate, how lucky you are, how hard it is to encounter the Great Compassion Mantra. Indeed, it is very hard to meet with the Great Compassion Mantra. Now that you have met it, remember: do not slight it and toss it aside.

Buddhist learners must spend some time studying the Buddhadharma, and not understand it vaguely and unclearly, seeming to know yet not knowing. Some think: "I already don't know, so I need not want to know. I already don't understand, so I'll just never understand." That is the attitude of one who surrenders, refusing to step forward, throwing away their own future.

For beginners setting out in cultivation, the greatest obstacle to applying effort is the mind of lust: boys craving girls, girls craving boys. This is the most basic issue.

Lecturing on sutras cultivates wisdom; sitting in meditation cultivates samadhi; keeping the mouth shut and speaking no idle words cultivates morality.

As humans in this world, we must do good at the right time, without delay. While a breath and a bit of strength remain, we must do good and accumulate virtue — not squander the wholesome roots planted in past lives by using up all our blessings in this one.

A cultivator who fears solitude cannot cultivate.

In our hearts there must never be ghosts. Nor hatred, resentment, gloom, or irritation. When these things exist, all is lost — for with them, ghosts have entered the house.

As a good spiritual teacher, you must not flatter people or scheme to please them, so that your friends grow deluded about the truth without even knowing it.

Ghost kings specialize in anger and never keep the rules. Guanyin Bodhisattva specializes in enduring humiliation and always keeps the rules.

Thinking about worthless things, you will reap worthless retribution in the future. All food and drink has but a single flavor. Dwelling on eating and drinking, the mind will run wild and the six senses cannot be reined in.

If the universe were filled with auspicious energy, the earth would not explode.

Take note: whatever states come from outside, pay them no heed, do not interfere with them — just let them be naturally, but never let them move your mind. The Shurangama Sutra explains this very clearly; I hope meditators will thoroughly study its section on the fifty skandha-demons.

A little sadness: touring the hells. One laugh: the old turn young. One bout of wailing: the hells gain a small, pitch-black room.

For cultivators the essential thing is to give rise to no afflictions, in any situation at all. Sitting, give rise to no afflictions; lying down, give rise to no afflictions. The key is to cut off afflictions. As the vow goes: afflictions are endless; I vow to transform them — to turn afflictions into enlightenment (bodhi). Affliction is non-awakening. Bodhi is awakening.

The Great Compassion Mantra is the great mantra of the great compassionate mind. It can penetrate heaven and earth. If you can recite it 108 times every day, continuously for three years, afterward you can use the Great Compassion Mantra to cure illness: where your hand reaches, illness is dispelled. I know of the Great Compassion Mantra's efficacy. I hope each of you will use the power of the Great Compassion Mantra to rescue the world from disaster (calamities and great trials), so that people may forever be free of calamities, and the Proper Dharma may dwell forever in the world.

The sages of old always blamed and corrected themselves — unlike people today, who never admit their own wrongs and always hunt for others' faults.

Each day we must talk a little less and recite the Buddha's name a little more. Beat the mind's thoughts to death, and the Dharma body will live. Talk less, recite more: as easy as turning over your hand.

Cultivators must go in reverse. What does that mean? It means: yield good things to others; shoulder bad things yourself. Cast away the small self to perfect the great self (the Buddha nature).

Want to study well, and karmic creditors will come looking. Want to become a Buddha, and you must meet demons. If you don't want to study the Way well, karmic creditors won't come looking for you. The better you want to study, the more they come — for they want to settle all the old debts.

Happy New Year! We need to be happy every year, every month, every day, every hour. Give rise to no afflictions — only then are you tending the plot of earth in the mind, nourishing the sky within your own nature.

As cultivators you must be genuine, stepping each step solidly, wasting not a single thought, advancing thought after thought along the path of the Way. Only then are you truly a Buddhist learner.

Cultivating the Way can increase wisdom, increase the resolve for enlightenment (bodhicitta), increase vows and strength. Everything, all things, increase.

Day after day, never forget the Ghost of Impermanence — no one knows when it will come to invite you along.

The Dharma-Ending Age is an age when demons are strong and the Dharma is weak. The demon kings' power grows ever greater. The Buddha's power shrinks ever smaller. Of the Buddha we should speak not of power but of awesome virtue. When beings have great blessings, the Dharma is strong and demons are weak. When beings have few blessings, demons are strong and the Dharma is weak.

If monastics crave offerings, covet food and clothing, then what Proper Dharma is left to speak of?

Single-mindedness brings spiritual response; a scattered mind brings blockage. How to be single-minded? You must cut off desire and abandon love. Without cutting off lust and love, a monastic may cultivate for eighty-four thousand great eons and still never succeed. Hence this point is supremely important.

Only without a greedy mind can you let go. With letting go comes freedom and ease, and afterward you can awaken and unfold great, perfect enlightenment.

We cultivators of the Way must turn being into nonbeing, returning to the root and the source — returning to our own inherent Buddha nature.

Liberation means graduating from the sphere of the Vinaya rules. It also means graduating from the sphere of regulations, graduating from the sphere of afflictions, graduating from the sphere of ignorance.

The essence of Dharma is emptiness, so you should not cling to dharmas. If toward dharmas you cannot see through and let go, you are still not free.

One with hatred in the heart will have a red-faced ghost.

One with resentment in the heart will have a yellow-faced ghost.

One with anguish in the heart will have a white-faced ghost.

One with rage in the heart will have a green-faced ghost.

One with vexation in the heart will have a black-faced ghost.

Hatred harms the heart. Resentment harms the spleen. Anguish harms the lungs. Rage harms the liver. Vexation harms the kidneys.

Children, while still physically immature, who go seeking objects of romantic love will damage (body and mind) and come to loss besides.

Cultivation need not seek high, faraway places. The Way is right before your eyes — within your own mind. The false mind is a galloping horse of intent, a leaping monkey of thought. Intent races like a horse; the mind jumps like a monkey. If you can recognize this mind, your cultivation will surely bring response.

Someone asked me: when you came to the West, how do you propagate the Buddhadharma? I replied: I rely entirely on Guanyin Bodhisattva, the Great Compassion Mantra, and the Shurangama Mantra.

Temples are places that nurture cultivators, not places that keep the lazy.

We must vie with one another to study the Buddhadharma. Studying the Buddhadharma is far more important than earning money. If you nurture your Dharma body and wisdom life strong and healthy, that is better than earning money by hundreds of thousands and millions.

Blessings must not be used up. Used up, no blessings remain. Suffering can be endured to its end. Endured to the end, suffering is over.

Reflect on the suffering of sickness, and health is a blessing.

Reflect on the suffering of disaster, and peace is a blessing.

Reflect on the suffering of having money, and having no money is a blessing.

Reflect on the suffering of wealth and rank, and poverty is a blessing.

From limitless eons past until now, we have been cheated by illusion. So life after life we must revolve in birth and death — like fish in a net, swimming in and out, never escaping the net. That, too, is because we refuse to bring forth the resolve for enlightenment (bodhicitta) and refuse to accept loss — so we must remain forever in birth and death, stuck in the wheel of rebirth turning through the six paths.

Those with genuine wisdom never praise themselves and disparage others. Whoever praises themselves has no future left. Though still alive, they are as good as dead.

In this life people keep seeking what is false, while throwing away what is true.

The whole world is filled with dark energy. Wherever there are people who truly cultivate, disasters there lessen and grow smaller. If many people cultivate together in one place, their collective strength can turn dark energy into auspicious energy.

Whoever lectures on the Dharma — no matter how great their spiritual powers — you must observe them. If they harbor greed, hunting for money everywhere, or harbor lust, then they are not genuine, but false. Only if they have no greed, no lust, no schemes, are they genuine.

Cultivation is not achieved in a day and a night. It requires day like this and night like this: the mind always practicing, firm and unchanging. After a long time it will develop into prajna wisdom. If you cultivate one day and rest ten days, you can never succeed.

In the temple, do not chatter idly. Nothing may be casual or careless. The rules are the Vinaya. Keeping the Vinaya brings purity. With purity you draw near to the Buddhas.

Our body is like a chemical factory, transforming in myriad ways. Sometimes it turns you into a worm, sometimes a bird, a hungry ghost — or, if the chemical reaction succeeds, turns you into a Buddha. It can turn being into nonbeing, nonbeing into being, transforming into countless different lives. Therefore be careful not to let it turn you into a hungry ghost or an animal. In this chemical factory we must smelt and forge ourselves into Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Hearers, and Those Enlightened by Conditions. A slight error in the transformation, and the result will differ vastly; wanting to turn back will not be easy.

Wanting to become a Buddha without cultivating: there is no such thing.

Ignorance means not understanding. The root of ignorance is lust and craving.

Do not think that having states is good. Having states without clearly recognizing them invites demons.

Whatever you encounter, never let that state move you; never chase after states. What to do? Regard them as if they did not exist. Whether meeting states or not meeting states, your mind must be the same. Give rise to neither delight nor aversion.

A great many worldly people only eat and wait for death, wasting their time. Everyone is the same: waking in the morning, bustling about this and that until climbing into bed at night — toiling all for three bowls of rice.
