Living like a walking lump of flesh, with not a shred of value or meaning — what difference is there between their living and dying?

Because people harbor hatred, there are fire disasters (conflagrations). Because of greed, there are water disasters (floods). Because of delusion, there are wind disasters (storms). The three disasters come from the three poisons of greed, anger, and delusion. Every one of us has all three poisons in the mind. If those minds grow stronger day by day, one day they will form a great calamity.

Outside there are computers; inside, our own nature also has a computer, called the divine brain, the sagely brain, or the Buddha brain — that is, great wisdom. Though science advances, its direction is outward, so the more it chases the truth, the farther it strays from the truth. Scientists apply effort only on the skin's surface, so they seem to gain something, when in fact they have forgotten their inherent wisdom. That is called abandoning the root for the branches.

In cultivating the Way you need not use force against obstacles. If you are sincere, all matters will naturally resolve smoothly.

You cannot wish to cultivate a world-transcending Dharma while refusing to let go of worldly dharmas. Standing with two feet on two boats — one boat heading north of the river, one heading south — that cannot be done.

If the poisons of the world are to be dispelled, everyone must eat vegetarian food and not eat meat.

Who is without attachments? Do not think that when you have nothing to do, you are free of attachments. Wait and see: when affairs come, when states arrive, how will you be? With nothing to do and no afflictions, that does not yet count as real. Only when states come and you can recognize them — that is what counts.

We Buddhist learners must deeply enter the sutra treasury — only then will wisdom be as vast as the sea. Without deeply entering the sutra treasury, wisdom can never be as vast and deep as the sea. Without deeply entering the sutra treasury, what will be like the sea? Your afflictions will be as wide as the sea. Your attachments will be as deep as the sea. Your wrong views will fill the sea. Therefore reading and reciting the Mahayana sutras is supremely important.

The ancients said: of the ten thousand evils, lust stands first. That is the road of death; it cannot be walked. Indulging in lust is like walking into the road of death.

Do not fail to do a good deed because it is too small; do not commit an evil deed because it is small either. However small a good deed, we must do it. However small an evil, we must not do it.

Cultivation means enduring hardship.

No contending, no greed, no seeking, no selfishness, no self-benefit, no lying: this is in fact very easy to do; no one forces you to do it. But because you refuse to do it, adversity arrives. That adversity is contending, greed, seeking, selfishness, self-benefit, lying. From these come unexpected calamities. When adversity arrives, you cannot bear it. Yet when you lie, why don't you feel equally unbearable?

Morality (shila) means: with every movement of mind, you must not give rise to anything evil or unwholesome.

Samadhi is the fruit of cultivating morality. If you keep the precepts long, you will gain samadhi power. Samadhi in Sanskrit is called samadhi or samapatti — right stillness, right abiding. Right stillness differs from deviant stillness. Right abiding differs from deviant abiding. Only right stillness and right abiding accord with the Proper Dharma. Deviant stillness and deviant abiding do not accord with the Dharma.

Through samadhi, wisdom unfolds. With wisdom we can recognize the Buddhadharma. Having recognized the Buddhadharma, we can become Buddhas. Thus cultivating morality, samadhi, and wisdom is the most basic condition for becoming a Buddha.

Why does the world grow worse by the day? Because everyone contends — contending for fame, for profit, for power, for position. Most serious of all is contending over sex.

Look: the great virtuous monks of a thousand years all cultivated amid hardship and austerity to attain the Way. Not one of them awakened through enjoyment. Read the entire Great Treasury of Sutras, and you will not find a single one.

If you can keep the three karmas of body, speech, and mind pure, then reciting the Buddha's name is like dropping a clearing jewel into muddy water. Muddy water cannot but clear. When the Buddha-reciting sound enters a scattered mind — a mind full of false thoughts — it will slowly dissolve along with the recitation, becoming solely the single sound of Buddha recitation.

Toward demons, do not regard them as enemies; regard them as good spiritual teachers helping you cultivate.

To study Buddhism, bring forth your true mind. In every move and act, every word and deed, head toward what is true.

Over many lives and eons we have created different karma, so our false thoughts are not the same either. Heavy karma means many false thoughts; light karma means few false thoughts. That is the ratio between karma and false thoughts.

In the temple, economize in everything, for: Cherish the monastery's property as you would guard your own eyes.

Neither love nor hate is the Middle Way. What is cultivation? It is precisely cultivating the Middle Way. Toward everyone deal equally, with caring compassion. Yet be careful in your actions: do not fall into the net of sentiment, the snare of love.

Our mind is where others (other people) dwell. It is not where we ourselves dwell. Because others dwell there, though we are present, our minds are not present.

Cultivators must restore the original emptiness. That is, return to the root and the source, perfecting our original nature — the treasury of great bright light — wisdom round and full like a mirror (the great perfect mirror wisdom), lacking nothing.

What is an earthquake? It is when lustful desire stirs. No earthquake is nirvana.

Some say: "My mind is old." This mind is born of the meeting of sense organs with sense objects — it is not the ever-abiding true mind, perfect, bright, still, and illumining. If you truly love living beings, sacrificing yourself for others, then however advanced in years, you will turn into youthful happiness.

In any situation, cultivators must know how to hide their light (conceal wisdom and talent); they must not show off, putting on airs of competence for others to see.

With attachment, that is the human mind. Without attachment, that is the mind of the Way.

The eyes contemplate Guanyin Bodhisattva before you, a thousand eyes watching over you, a thousand hands protecting you. The ears hear the name "Namo Guanshiyin Bodhisattva" and carry it into the mind. The mouth recites her name clearly, word by word. Remember her clearly too. At all six senses — ear, eye, nose, tongue, body, mind — you should recite Guanyin.

Without merit and virtue, death will be very painful.

In cultivation you must not wear masks — hanging up a sheep's head while selling dog meat, doing things untrue and contrary to reason. Cultivation must be genuine: step firmly, truly apply effort.

The Great Compassion Mantra and Guanyin Bodhisattva are two, yet not two; not two, yet two. The two cannot be separated. I hope all good spiritual teachers can sincerely recite the Great Compassion Mantra, to dispel disasters and calamities.

In cultivation you must not peddle your cultivation, nor advertise yourself. Peddling your cultivation invites demonic obstacles.

Buddha and demon are only one thought apart. The Buddha has compassion; demons have the will to outdo and outwin.

Heaven and earth are born from the Middle Way. The Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Arhats are also born from the Middle Way. The Middle Way is the common mother of Buddhas and sages. Inclining neither to emptiness nor to being, cultivate the Middle Way Dharma with unbroken concentration. Chan meditation, sitting with a settled mind — all are cultivating the Middle Way Dharma. In terms of form, the Middle Way is the number one; in terms of formlessness, the Middle Way is the number zero. Emptiness is the ultimate meaning of the Middle Way.

Cultivation must be沉沉 calm and quiet. No afflictions, no arrogance.

Buddhist learners must make Buddhism ever more radiant and resplendent. How? First, possess virtuous character, a will vast as empty space, a heart as boundless as the Dharma Realm.

Why is it said that if your mind has no ghosts, outer ghosts cannot harm you? Outer ghosts exist because your mind has ghosts. If your mind has no ghosts, outer ghosts will not come. The inner ghosts are of five kinds: greed, anger, delusion, pride, and doubt. They are also the five: hatred, resentment, anguish, rage, and vexation.

We refuse to bring forth wisdom. Day after day we use only the strength of ignorant afflictions. Touched slightly, the fire of anger flares up. As the saying goes: the fire of ignorance, the tiger-spirit! Anger comes from the roots of offenses in past lives. Without offenses there would be no fire of ignorance. When the fire of ignorance erupts, greed, anger, and delusion all arrive in full. Turn the light around and shine upon yourselves, and see if this is not so.

Ignorance has two accomplices that join it as a gang. Who are they, ultimately? First, food and drink; second, lust and sex. One is craving food and drink. The other is lusting after beauty, craving sex. These two help ignorance do every evil deed.

Arrive at the point of seeking nothing, and worries end. Know fewer things, and afflictions lessen.

Whatever state you face, your attitude must be: having is as if not having; true is as if false. Remember: do not gain a little and deem it enough; do not take the false for real.

Food and drink increase desire. Desire increases ignorance.

Bodhisattvas fear causes, not results; ordinary people fear results, not causes. While still planting causes, Bodhisattvas are utterly careful, never acting recklessly in the least. When retribution arrives, they do not fear. But ordinary people, when sowing causes, fear nothing: killing, stealing, lust, lying, drink, gambling, smoking opium and taking drugs — these you dare to think and dare to do; only when reaping retribution do you cry out in suffering.

In this world, whether eating, dressing, or sleeping, we are always within the scope of the Buddhadharma. Pity that we do not know how to experience the Buddhadharma in daily life, always seeking outwardly. What is a follower of side-door paths? One who seeks the Dharma outside the mind.

No one should look down on themselves, throw themselves away, and willingly consent to fall.

Whether you break precepts of the body — killing, stealing, lust; or break precepts of speech — lying, divisive speech, flowery speech, harsh speech; or break precepts of the mind — giving rise to greed, anger, delusion: you must sincerely repent. Otherwise you will sink into the mire, sinking deeper and deeper, offenses growing ever graver. You will be pressed until you cannot breathe, with no escape.

You should know: living in this world, we are like fish in a puddle fast drying up. Before long — alas! — the water will run dry. From limitless eons until today, we have not known how to cultivate: born, then dying; dead, then born again. How heartbreaking! Why, even today, do we still hesitate and wait, refusing to cultivate?

Lust and craving are birth and death. Birth and death are the mind of lust and craving. Lust and craving are the root of birth and death. Without cutting off lust, craving, and ignorance, you can never escape the sea of love-driven birth and death.

Why do inauspicious things happen? Because the mind is inauspicious. Once you plant a bad cause, you will reap a bad result. If you can reform your faults and do good, you can turn evil into good. From this we see: destiny can be changed; it rests entirely in your own hands. Hence: great good and great evil transcend destiny.

There is no such thing as becoming a Buddha without cutting off lust. No such thing exists under heaven. People today mostly love speed, love instant results, so when they hear of a wondrous Dharma they are bewitched and fall into the demons' net. At death they still believe in secret dharmas, esoteric methods! Secret? Secret! Secret all the way into the hells!

Cultivate with a mind like a newborn babe: nothing lingering in the heart. Be like an infant — you must return to youth from old age. But returning to youth does not mean drinking milk like a child; it means sweeping clean greed, anger, delusion, pride, and doubt. That is called returning to the root and the source: your mind like a child's, innocent and lively, without a trace of laziness, without a thought of vying to win, without notions of self and others. Just like: fundamentally not a single thing exists — then where can dust alight?

One sentence about you, and you are upset, displeased. Touch a single hair and it hurts you to the heart. They even say: pull out one hair to benefit the world — and you refuse. With such selfishness, no cultivation is possible. Cultivators of the Way must have no notion of self or others, no notion of living beings or of a life span.

The biggest leak is lustful leakage — the mind of lust. With lustful thoughts, it is like thieves coming to steal, carrying off all your treasures. It is like timber eaten by termites, rendering the wood useless. It is like fine food with a bit of excrement dropped in — no one dares eat it. Three days of vomiting, no less!

Monastics must painfully remember the question of birth and death and bring forth the resolve for enlightenment (bodhicitta). They cannot eat their fill and wait for death. As the saying goes: a day as a monk, a day of striking the bell. A monk with such a mentality has no mastery at all over his own birth and death.

We must fiercely resolve to wash our hearts and change our ways, smash superstitious attitudes, and wipe out selfish, self-benefiting ways.

I offer the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas to all humanity and to all Buddhist followers in the whole world.

Never spend the day gloomy, unable to lift your brows. Look at everything lightly, as dream, as illusion. Handle all matters calmly and with ease. Everything in the world is false; you need only do your duty wholeheartedly, and that is enough. Everyone born into the world comes only to repay debts.

Turn the light around and reflect; seek the answer within yourself. See how many wholesome thoughts you have given rise to, how many evil thoughts, how many false thoughts. Wholesome thoughts not yet born — bring them forth. Wholesome thoughts already born — make them grow. Evil thoughts not yet born — do not give birth to them. Evil thoughts already born — extinguish them. Do not be casual and careless, wasting time and life. False thoughts that have value but cannot be realized — do not dally over them. False thoughts with no value at all — of course, do not think of them. One who truly knows how to apply effort constantly checks himself. Walking, standing, sitting, lying — never apart from home (the true mind, the resolve for enlightenment).

In this world, if you cannot throw away the false, you cannot accomplish the true. Without casting off death (false thoughts, attachments), you cannot exchange it for life (wisdom, freedom). If you wish not to die, be a dead person while living. That is: though alive, regard yourself as dead (no more vying, no more greed...) — and then you will truly understand:

All conditioned dharmas,

like dreams, illusions, bubbles, shadows;

like dew, like lightning flashes,

contemplate them thus.

Our greed, anger, and delusion are very hard to douse, hard to wipe out — and all the more must we douse and wipe them out. If wiping them out were too easy, we would hardly need to spend strength and effort.

In giving, give to the Triple Jewel. It is not for the Triple Jewel to give to you.

False thoughts are stones tied to the cultivator's feet, obstructing the accomplishment of the Way.

Money is nothing but a slip of paper printed with gaudy pictures. Yet that colored slip deludes people, making them forget kindness, righteousness, and morality. All because they crave these paper slips, taking them for real. Are you deluded or not?

Anger is heated temper, and it is affliction too. With an angry heart, everyone you see is bad. If one person wrongs me, I flare up at everyone. It is just like taking afflictions for food: eat one bowl, then another bowl. Finish, then eat yet another bowl. Forever, never eating your fill.

Delusion is a foolish mind of false thinking and folly. Taking what you may not take is delusion. Eating what you may not eat is delusion. Wanting what you may not have is delusion. Doing what you may not do is delusion.

However dazzlingly beautiful a person may be, they are only a bag of stinking skin. However ugly, also only a bag of stinking skin. Outside they differ, but inside they are the same — nothing beautiful or ugly about it. Look deeper within, and it is all blood, pus, phlegm, drool, filth. Examine the five organs, and it is all excrement and urine. Fair outside, unbearably foul inside — what difference is there? Why cling to this body! The deluded prize outer beauty, clinging to fine, lovely marks while hating ugly marks. Is this not delusion?

Cultivators must remember never to crave fine food and enjoyment. At all times take Shakyamuni Buddha's practice as your mirror to encourage and warn yourself. Never, at any moment, indulge.

Men and women alike, in cultivation, must completely cut off the seven emotions. What are the seven emotions? Joy, anger, sorrow, fear, love, hatred, and craving. Ruled by these seven, your samadhi power will vanish. When states blow like wind, your mind will waver, masterless — like a house with no owner — and that is upside-down confusion.

In this world, doing anything wrong is like living in hell. Doing anything contrary to reason, with a selfish, self-benefiting mind, is already dwelling in hell. Delighting in this affair, raging at that matter, always solving problems with emotions — that too is dwelling in hell.

What is upside-down confusion? Taking suffering for joy, right for wrong, unable to tell black from white, true from false; taking the impermanent for the permanent.

Cultivators must be honest with one another, encouraging one another, guiding one another toward brightness. You cannot collude in evil, shield wickedness, or flatter and fawn over people, acting as their servants.

The sea of suffering is boundless; turning back is the shore. Do not sink and drift forever in the sea of suffering. Then there will never be a day of liberation.

Our body is utterly filthy. Yet people treat it like a treasure, hanging it with diamonds and jewels, anointing it with perfume and rouge. Is that not taking treasures and flowers to decorate a privy?

Cultivators of the Way must sweep clean all false thoughts of the seven emotions and six desires. Sweep them utterly clean.

Why is it said the three minds cannot be grasped? The past mind cannot be grasped; the present mind cannot be grasped; the future mind cannot be grasped. The past has already passed; passed, and what is left? With no past, thinking of it cannot hold it. The present does not abide: thought after thought flows by, thought after thought moves, thought after thought never pausing — so the present mind cannot be grasped either. The future has not yet come — what can you do with it? So the future mind cannot be grasped either. If you can grasp none of the three minds, and give rise to none of the four marks of attachment (to self, to others, to living beings, to a life span), then you can unite with your own nature, perfect enlightenment (bodhi), and return to the place of nothing attained.

In cultivation, whatever thought you harbor, a corresponding ghost will come. Ghosts are a kind of yin energy. With wholesome thoughts, the yin energy dissolves. If you reform your ways of thinking, letting light shine in, there will be wisdom.

Though all beings say with their lips that they seek peace and joy, alas — the more they seek, the more they suffer.

When people reform evil and do good, the world will have no more three disasters and eight calamities. Good people treating one another with kindness, neither contending nor craving — the world will become a world of great oneness.

We Buddhist cultivators of the Way should not calculate too much. Someone scolds me — but who am I? Someone hits me — but who am I? Ask yourself, and you will find no self at all. Then why not let go of it?

In cultivation you must turn wisdom's light to shine upon your own heart, asking yourself: do I harbor greed? If so, that is not cultivation. If not, that is cultivation. Ask yourself: do I harbor hatred? If so, that is not cultivation. If not, it proves the self has lessened a little. Beaten, regard it as unseen; scolded, see through it with reason. If affliction stirs within and anger flares, cultivation is impossible. Ask yourself: am I deluded? Have I understood one thing so as to understand all, with no obstruction? As the saying goes: true emptiness holds no self or others; the great Way has no marks.

Those with deep good roots heed wholesome words. Those with heavy offenses heed slanderous words.

Without throwing away the false, the true can never be attained. Why? Because chasing after the tail of the false, how can you recognize the face of the true?

With afflictions come heat. Without afflictions comes coolness. Who told you to give rise to afflictions?

Let go of body and mind, and Buddhahood is naturally accomplished.

Bring forth the resolve for enlightenment (bodhicitta); benefit living beings. Do not learn the narrow ways of the Two Vehicles, caring only for yourselves in selfishness, refusing to save others.

Managing the assembly's food and drink, those in charge must know how to balance meals — only then is there merit. Without knowing how to balance properly, sloppy and careless, there is karmic offense. Accord with the rules, and there is merit; against the rules, there is fault. Careful not to waste food, and there is merit. Squandering food, and there is offense.

The Middle Way holds no joy, sorrow, anger, fear, love, hatred, or craving. If none of these seven emotions stir waves, then within your heart there are no false thoughts, and without you chase nothing. When body and mind within and without are pure — that is the realm of nature-samadhi.

The seven emotions are like breakers on the ocean. If waves surge, boats will surely capsize. With winds stopped and waves calm, ships land safely. So cultivators must see through these seven emotions. Seeing through their meaning is not enough — you must have the power to master their pull, taming them so they cannot misbehave. Unmoved by the seven emotions — only that is called nature-samadhi.

When matters come, meet them — but without the slightest opportunistic, scrambling mind. (The scrambling mind is the monkey mind that climbs and claws: calculating, selfish, forever seeking profit and connections, ceaselessly plotting for self.) When matters pass, leave no trace in the heart; keep the heart pure. See clearly that the three mind-states of past, present, and future cannot be held. Having seen through, cultivate accordingly — only then do you truly understand the Buddhadharma.

The greatest taboo in study and cultivation is starting the head without finishing the tail — quitting halfway down the road. Then the work already done is abandoned midstream, never moving forward, and the precious treasury can never be reached.

Remember: whatever you do, finish head and tail. Never let outer conditions move your mind and make you abandon your vows. Set vows firm as stone, solid as bronze; let no adversity shake them or make you forget bodhicitta.

Buddhist learners should believe in cause and effect, for cause and effect never errs by a hair. Never mistake the sowing of causes and reaping of fruits; never slander cause and effect as nonexistent. Understand: cause and effect is the unchanging law of a thousand ages.

All who dwell at the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas must honor one another. Do not stand by indifferent to others' fate. Learn the spirit of the Bodhisattvas: seeing beings suffer amid burning fire and drowning water, they feel as if they themselves suffered. So they seek ways to bring beings out of the sea of suffering.

Know a little, cultivate a little. Gathering small makes great; piling sand makes pagodas. When the work suffices, accomplishment comes.

Do not miss precious time and opportunity; do not fail the hopes of teachers and friends. Bravely, vigorously cultivate the unsurpassed Way, and soon accomplish Buddhahood.

Rendering service (doing what benefits beings on the path), and setting down words (writing, teaching, adding to later generations' understanding and wisdom) in Buddhism — only then are you truly a child of the Buddha.

Turning back from the realm of delusion is awakening.

Cultivators must never let the fire of anger flare in heart and liver. Be patient; for: the fire of ignorance burns clean the forest of merit and virtue. Remember this well.

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas hold this in their hearts: giving kindness without asking return, giving without ever regretting. They cherish kindness toward the affinity-less, great compassion regarding others as self. Through such cultivation they gained transcendent wisdom and unfathomable spiritual powers.

Everyone knows dwelling in the Three Realms is unsafe, like living in a burning house. Yet no one will let go of the Three Realms. Knowing full well the burning-house Three Realms bring ten thousand pains, still they linger on within, utterly unafraid, unalarmed — even idly deeming it great fun.

Wherever you are, make offerings to the Triple Jewel. Never hunt for the Triple Jewel's faults with a nitpicking, hair-splitting attitude. Fault-hunting is arrogance, not the attitude of one who guards the Triple Jewel.

All day the six senses chase the six objects, never turning the light around to shine within — that is called outflow.

What is the treasure within the house? This treasure is no worldly gold, silver, or jewels. It is the ever-abiding true mind — the Tathagata Treasury — the bright, subtle, awakened nature.

Worldly people bustle and struggle all day over nothing but money-making, food, clothing, shelter, fame, and profit. All are driven mad by these five; from morning to night there is no rest. Off work, at home they watch TV, movies, play on computers, go touring. Plenty to keep everyone busy all the time.

You should know the Shurangama Sutra is the Buddha's true body — that is, the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, and the Vinaya; it is precisely morality, samadhi, wisdom. If you wish to honor the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, first honor the Shurangama Sutra.

In this dusty world, the three teachings and nine schools, people of all directions and virtues, all beings with shape and form, with deeds and karma — all want to plan for life; none want to plan for death. No one thinks how they will die in the future. Living — well, they are living now; but dying — what will it be? Because no one thinks of this, it is said that no one plans for death.

In all things keep measure; never go to extremes.

The morning and evening recitation sessions are public duties; no one in a Way-place may shirk them. Skipping these daily sessions disdains the Way-place, disdains the Buddhas and the abbot. Disdaining the abbot, you may not dwell in the temple.

The cultivator's secret: eat little.

Cultivating without reforming faults is like not cultivating at all.

Temple goods may not be casually given to outsiders. Thinking this earns merit, you are in fact stealing from the Sangha. Taking public property to bestow privately and curry favor is conduct that wrecks the Way-place's rules.

As a rule, all merit created must be transferred to beings in the Dharma Realm. Otherwise you become selfish.

Where there is the Shurangama Sutra, there is the Buddhadharma. To guard the Buddhadharma, first of all propagate the Shurangama Sutra. Memorize the sutra, learn to explain it; then cultivate according to its principles.

Losing the true mind, you will sink into the sea of suffering, unable to get out.

Monastics should know: while the work of the Way is unfinished, do not go into debt. In debt, you will be bound and cannot be liberated. Especially impure affinities will harm you, leaving you unable to pull your feet out, unable to be free.

As humans, all must pass through birth, aging, sickness, death — the four great sufferings. Everyone must bear these sufferings. Unless you cultivate the Way and end birth and death.

Good spiritual friends! Remember the pain of birth and death, and bring forth the resolve for enlightenment (bodhicitta). Drift no more in the sea of suffering. Whoever will not leave the sea of suffering is a fool.

Everything in the world is interrelated. Like the three teachings — Buddhist, Taoist, Confucian — closely bound to one another. Confucianism is like elementary school. Taoism is like middle school. Buddhism is like university.

Living beings means born of the union of conditions. Living beings are not only humans, but all that lives.

Worldly affairs are truly strange. The less people have, the greedier they are. The more they have, the less they can let go.

The hot-tempered are the deluded.

The rich are those who dislike taking advantage. The truly wealthy never like grabbing the upper hand or bullying others. Those who love the upper hand are the truly poor.

Being human is truly dangerous. Being a Buddha is truly safe. If you like danger, do dangerous deeds. If you want safe, happy peace, do safe, happy, peaceful deeds.

In ordinary times you must know how to recite the Buddha's name, cultivating the Pure Land method. At life's end you will not panic or flounder, but peacefully go to rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

At death, however rich you are, you cannot buy deathlessness.

When people receive the five precepts, each precept they keep brings five Dharma-protecting spirits to guard them. Break the precepts, and those five spirits run off. In their place, five evil spirits arrive.

Turning back to seek the answer within yourself means truly admitting your own errors, saying nothing of others' faults.

Some people in past lives created a great deal of killing karma — hunting, netting fish, slaughtering chickens, butchering oxen, bleeding pigs, killing dogs. Because they created so much killing karma, in this life they suffer every strange, hard-to-cure illness.

The Buddhadharma is inseparable from each person's mind — so the Buddhadharma is precisely mind-Dharma. If your mind holds no selfishness, false thoughts, arrogance, wild ambition, or bad habits, then that is the Buddhadharma.

Vigor does not mean eating more than others. Nor does it mean working less than others, snoring before others sleep, and still unwake when others have risen. Nor is it vigorously chasing fame and profit — it is vigorously bringing forth the great resolve for enlightenment (bodhicitta).

The Ghost of Impermanence cares nothing for old or young: when the time comes to lead you to King Yama, it will show no courtesy. As the saying goes: Above ground, neither old nor young; below ground, all constantly meet. (In this world the god of death spares neither old nor young. In the underworld, everyone constantly meets him.)

If you like hearing sutras, urge others to come and hear them too.

Going against the yin and yang of heaven and earth brings incurable, terminal illness.

In cultivation, never make excuses for yourself, never twist arguments evasively, and never gossip about rights and wrongs (discussing others' good and bad, right and wrong).

Without beings there would be no sutras. Without sutras there would be no teaching beings to become Buddhas.

If anyone scolds me (the monk), bow to them. Whoever slanders me, never defend me.

The more money you save up for your descendants, the greater the calamity you rear for them. Saving little money for them instead avoids much trouble.

Waste no time. With free hours, apply effort. Strive on, vigorously and diligently.

Guarding the Dharma means not letting the Dharma perish.

Whoever lectures on the Dharma, well or poorly, never feel disgust, affliction, or irritation toward them.

Not cultivating young, then waiting till gray-haired to cultivate — too late.

When your mind holds no attachments, Buddha images are consecrated (their eyes "opened") at all times. With an attached mind, even a consecrated image is no different from unconsecrated.

Eating a little less meat means a little less strange illness.

The rule of life is knowing root and source: devoting yourself wholeheartedly, utterly filial to your parents, reverent to teachers and elders. That is the natural law of heaven and earth.

Hearing no sutra lectures on the Dharma, only burying your head in cultivation — that is called blind cultivation, reckless training. Though you cultivated for eons as countless as dust motes, you could never succeed.

The good bear halos of white light. The evil reek with dark, black energy. So good and evil naturally show in outer marks. You can fool people's eyes, but never the eyes of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, ghosts, and spirits.

Hearing no sutra lectures, yet reading trashy books and papers — that is already breaking the rules.

Because you hear lectures without understanding, you must keep hearing. If you heard and understood, you would not need to hear at all.

What are mountains? Our own arrogance. What are seas? Our sense of inferiority, deeming ourselves low. With pride come high mountains. With self-belittling come deep seas.

Why must we gather the light back in, not shining it outward? Take an oil lamp: lit, its light spreads. But burning on and on, the oil runs dry and the lamp dies. Lit only when needed, snuffed when unused, the lamp lasts very long. (Do not squander your light — wisdom and talent; know how to preserve it. Do not let fame and profit lure you into using up your potential.)

The Buddha radiates light to smash beings' ignorance.

Propagating the Buddhadharma is everyone's task; all should share the load. Those with money give money; those with strength give strength. We must strive, united as one — only then can Buddhism flourish.

Eating meat makes desires many and false thoughts many; samadhi is very hard to enter. Not eating meat keeps desires light, the heart content, false thoughts fewer. That is because our blood and energy grow light, not turbid.

One who knows how to chant sutras knows how to chant not only sutras with words, but also wordless sutras. Only one who can chant wordless sutras truly understands the Buddhadharma.

Ultimately, what is a wordless sutra? It is when you give rise to not a single thought. Giving rise to no thought, you return to still emptiness.

People in the world have a cutting saying: Monastics don't crave money — but the more, the better! Monastics hearing this must reflect and examine themselves: do I hold such thoughts? If so, reform; if not, beware.

With one Buddha recitation, the lotus blooms a little bigger. Reciting thought after thought, all "Namo Amitabha Buddha," the lotus blooms as big as a wheel. When you are reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, your spiritual nature will dwell within that lotus.

The Saha world is shrouded in ten thousand sufferings, teeming with ten thousand evils. All quarrel with one another; never a moment of peace. In Ultimate Bliss there are no afflictions, no troubles at all. So we must seek rebirth in the Pure Land — born by transformation from a lotus, meeting Amitabha face to face, attaining the stage of non-retreat.

Many act as servants to this body — late to bed, early to rise. Why? For whom is all this bustle, ultimately? For yourself? For others? I believe many cannot answer this question.

Know this: the noble person thinks only of the Way, not of food and drink.

In Buddhism, dealing with people or handling affairs, always rely on kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity — the four boundless minds. Never borrow public matters to avenge private grudges. Never, over some discord, nitpick and hunt for others' faults. Always settle public affairs with a straight heart — no hatred, no bias.

Striking the wooden fish in rhythm brings merit. Striking the wooden fish in anger — banging thunderously, or tapping faintly — is all offense.

Because past lives created karmic obstacles, there are times in this life when ghosts come to collect debts. Such times are when one's yang energy is weak — yin waxing, yang waning — and ghosts seize the chance. If you constantly harbor not a shred of affliction, with wisdom ever present, ghosts will find no gap to slip in and harm you.

Truly reciting the Buddha's name means: walking, standing, sitting, lying — you know only "Namo Amitabha Buddha," the six-syllable sacred name. Watching water flow and knowing water flows, watching wind blow and knowing wind blows, gazing east then staring west, surveying motion and stillness everywhere — that is not truly reciting the Buddha's name.

Blatantly showing off (talent, wisdom) is truly foolish conduct.

Life is not money; it is a priceless treasure. Life cannot be bought and sold with money. Yet some in the world sell their lives cheap, gladly sacrificing life and limb for coins. In society — whether among the three teachings and nine schools, people of all directions and virtues — for money they will sell their very souls and lives.

Greatly public-spirited and selfless means no selfishness, no self-benefit, no desires. Toward money, beauty, fame, food, and sleep — utterly unattached, neither craving nor loving.

Past-life cultivation makes this life go smoothly in everything. Cultivating in this life makes the next life better still. Without cultivation, the future can never match this life. Whether later lives go well or ill is decided entirely by yourself. Buddhas and Bodhisattvas cannot help you.

A bowl of soup full of meat and fish (though small) holds hatred and enmity as deep as the sea. That enmity can never be told to its end.

Meat holds a kind of turbid energy. That is because it comes from turbid things. So meat-eaters can hardly keep precepts, hardly unfold wisdom, hardly gain samadhi.

Some do not treat studying the Buddhadharma as important; family matters come first. They say: "I must fulfill my duties first." When they die, who shoulders those duties? Clearly they cannot reckon!

Cultivation is not just the morning and evening recitation sessions. Ordinarily, in every move and act, every word and deed, keep rhythm and measure. For everyone has the music of their own nature.

With an unpeaceful mind, you need outer music to tune the inner mood. If your mind were ever calm and harmonious, filled with a concordant, blissful air — that would be genuine music.

You have come to the jeweled mountain; do not go home empty-handed.

For scolding and slander, harbor no hatred. Regard foe and kin alike, meeting them with kindness. Otherwise, how can you display the power of compassion born of patience with the non-arising of dharmas (realizing the emptiness of self, others, and all dharmas)?

Each day reflect: how much time spent scheming for myself, how much for others? How much for the temple? Reflecting thus, you will know whether you have smashed clinging to self.

Reflect: how is your skill in patience? Groundlessly insulted or beaten by others, can you endure? Will you flare up? Will hatred and revenge arise? If so, clinging to self remains, unremoved.

I urge you who are rich: do public-good, virtuous deeds; rescue the world and save lives. That is limitless merit!

Some think: when I am old, will I starve or freeze? Such thoughts are truly petty.

Do you know: refusing to let go, refusing to give, without sympathy, not knowing pity — that is why we revolve unceasingly in birth and death.

The Diamond Sutra teaches: One should give rise to the mind, dwelling nowhere. With a "place" (an object, a thought, a feeling), there is dwelling. Dwelling nowhere means thinking neither good nor evil. Apply effort right here. If the mind fastens on something, thinking good or ill of it — that is clinging, entanglement.

Some religions claim everything is ruled by a god. If ruled by a god, then doing good or evil has nothing to do with us. But when retribution falls, we must bear it — the god cannot help. This is unreasonable.

Beings' minds are like lamp switches: switch on, and the Buddha's light shines. Switch off, and the Buddha's halo cannot shine.

Monastics should dwell together in a great monastery (large temple), cultivating the Way together, encouraging and waking one another. Dwelling alone in a small house (a hut), if you do not apply effort, no one checks on you. Eating well, no one speaks. Eating meat, drinking wine — no trouble at all. Lay donors think (living alone) is great merit, when in fact they only help such monastics fall into the hells.

Whatever meat you eat sustains your body's life. Over long time, your body's energy becomes wholly the energy of those meats: pig energy, cow energy... Your blood becomes their blood too. So your flesh turns into their flesh. I ask the wise to think deeply on this.

Never go about speaking others' faults: "They did this wrong, that awry." Doing so, you plant the seed of suffering (against the law of cause and effect).

What, then, is the resolve for enlightenment (bodhicitta)? That mind is formless and markless — simply awakening.

Think honestly: where do all troubles and afflictions come from? All from clinging to the self.

Monastics need lofty, outstanding character. Do not drift with the times, eating your fill in idleness, making Buddhism's vigor sink into gloom, without a shred of radiance.

Why may laypeople not accept offerings? Because, not having left home, you are not among the Triple Jewel (only the Triple Jewel receives offerings). You cannot invent a fourth jewel (a Fourth Jewel) of your own.

Many do not understand what the Triple Jewel is. Some laypeople even want to set up a Fourth Jewel. Then it is not laypeople offering to the Triple Jewel, but the Triple Jewel offering to laypeople! Soon there may be a Fifth Jewel, a Sixth, a Seventh...! If this is not the face of the Dharma-Ending Age, what is it?

Do not kill! All beings, from beginningless eons until now, have all been our parents, kin, and kinfolk. Past lives' parents may have created offenses and in this life fallen as pigs, oxen, goats, horses... If you slaughter animals at will, you indirectly kill your own parents.

Follow nature; grow according to physiological law (for nature is most moderate, orderly, harmonious). Do not eat erratically or talk wildly. Drink, smoke, take drugs and opium, even abuse seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and thinking — all these harm your body and your spiritual nature.

Meeting those who gossip and slander you — however wronged you are — endure it. All are karmic debts of past lives, come to collect in this one. So you cannot refuse to pay. Debts paid in full, and the sky turns blue and clear: no more afflictions, no more worries.

The six principles — no contending, no greed, no seeking, no selfishness, no self-benefit, no lying — are the Dharma treasure that cuts off desires and wins you true wisdom.

Not only sitting in meditation and bowing to the Buddha is cultivation. Eating, dressing, every move and act is all cultivation.

Cultivators must: know only the plowing, ask nothing of the harvest. Whatever you do, do it wholeheartedly, with all your strength; never calculate what benefit the result will bring.

If all day you waste no words and think no idle thoughts; you tune your mood to calm and natural ease — unbound, unhindered, no self or others, no rights or wrongs — is that not music?

The character self plus the character great makes the character stinking (foul). Arrogant and self-great, you will stink to high heaven; no one will dare come near. All will hold their noses and flee, daring not approach.

The great Shurangama samadhi is not trained up by sitting in meditation. While walking, standing, sitting, or lying, if outer states cannot move your mind and false thoughts cannot disturb you — that is samadhi.

Do not fear poverty. Poverty does not hinder the Way. Fear only demons: demons are wrong knowledge and wrong views (mistaken, deviant understanding and views of the truth). With wrong knowledge and views, no Dharma door you cultivate will accord.

If the eight winds — praise, blame, bitterness, sweetness, gain, loss, disgrace, honor — can move your mind, then your foundation in cultivation is not yet firm.

The young must not be bound by filth. Hold this attitude: however cold, bare your chest to meet the wind like heroes; however hungry, puff out your bellies and march on. Be bright torches in fierce winds, true gold in blazing fire. Fear nothing.

Dedicated students of the Way, whoever lectures — well or poorly — fix their eyes and gather their spirits, reverently listening. The inattentive will doze off. That is the trial tempering true and false.

(Saving up) great fortunes, your descendants will grow very bold: fearing nothing, doing as they please until the family fortune is squandered — only then stopping. Leaving small fortunes, your descendants will stay timid: content with everything, (unambitious), and so troubles are few.

Worldly people's success is the sages' failure. So your ledger (of karma) must be settled clearly. Be a clear-eyed person. Once clear-eyed, forever clear-eyed. Smash through the gate of birth and death; jump out of birth and death's wheel. That is truly the work of a great hero.

The noble person seeks the answer within himself. The petty person seeks it in others. The petty are always outward-bound.

Life after life we drift in the sea of suffering. Wishing to cultivate, yet unable to throw away our garbage. Never willing to be pure and dust-free. Truly pitiful.

Helping others is the wellspring of joy and happiness. If you always deem helping others as important as helping yourself, the world will be most peaceful and stable.

Many make vegetarian dishes shaped like chicken, duck, or fish, because they cannot forget the taste of meat. They crave a taste. They say eating mock meat eases the craving, cheating the palate. In Buddhism, this bad habit must be reformed. Unreformed, after long time perhaps no monastic will eat vegetarian food at all.

I hold that once vegetarian, even dish names should hold no chicken or duck. I hope every Buddhist follower will have the eye that knows truth (the Dharma-discerning eye). Understand cause and effect; never mistake the sowing of causes and reaping of fruits.

Eating vegetarian, eat purely; stop longing for meaty flavors. Shaping food into birds and fish (though mock) is no different from humiliating Buddhism. Followers who do not see clearly casually approve. At root, that is lack of wisdom — no eye for truth, no insight into cause and effect, only hazy delusion.

When animals are slaughtered, their hearts fill with vengeful poison. At death's door, frightened and hateful, they long for revenge. That hateful, vengeful mindset breeds toxins — and meat-eaters eat those very toxins.

People meet sudden disasters and calamities all through speaking wildly (irresponsible, vicious, nonsensical words...).

Everything in the world is most subtle, but few recognize it. For example: selling fake medicine does brisk business, while selling real medicine goes begging. Why? Because few truly recognize real medicine's worth.

If I translated all the sutras into every language, bringing the Buddhadharma into everyone's heart — only that would be everlasting work.

Why are small temples no good? Because there, nothing restrains you. Eat, dress, sleep, walk as you please; the Way is easily forgotten. Every day knows only scrambling for connections. This habit deals Buddhism a mortal blow.

Some doubt: is there really a King Yama and a Ghost of Impermanence?

Just see whether you will die. If you never die, then there is no Ghost of Impermanence. If you confidently assert you undergo no retribution, then there is no King Yama.

With samadhi power, movement and stillness are not two (no different). Amid motion, unruled by it — that is stillness. Amid stillness, untroubled by false thoughts — that is motion. If you cultivate until motion and stillness are one, your skill fuses into a single mass. Then it is neither motion nor stillness, neither empty nor existent. That is precisely the Middle Way.

Never delight in hearing praise and flattery. Never intoxicate yourself, never advertise yourself.

Knowing how to repent, reforming into a new person, recognizing your own faults, untying the knots of offenses created — offenses melt clean away. Like sickness that breaks into sweat: the illness slowly eases, then fully heals.

This age is called the space age. Ultimately, what is space? Space means seeing through all things, letting go of everything, reaching freedom.

Clinging to goods and property, even to food and clothing, means clinging to wealth, sex, fame, food, and sleep. Then it is no longer great emptiness but great existence! (The word "great" also means "excessive": no longer excessively empty, but excessively existent!)

When you have nothing left at all, you restore your original face.

Why do you lack wisdom and spiritual powers? Because you keep running about gathering garbage. Jewels and treasures you disdain; inherent riches unwanted, tossed away. Yet you still deem yourself so clever! Truly, utter delusion.

With offenses, refusing to reform and instead hiding them so none know: that is offense piled upon offense.

Without the Shurangama Mantra in the world, demon-ghosts and goblins do as they please, fearing nothing, running rampant at will. While the Shurangama Mantra remains, side-door deviant paths, goblins and sprites, mountain goblins and water monsters still fear, daring not openly appear in the world.

Cultivating without vowing is like a tree that blooms but never bears fruit. It will not do.

Whatever we meet and undergo in life all comes from past-life karma. To change your own destiny, do a great many meritorious and virtuous deeds.

The Buddha holds no anger. Only demons do.

Where do demons come from? From five poisons: hatred, resentment, affliction, rage, and vexation.

Set great aims; do great deeds. Do not dream of becoming officials and earning heaps of money. That only feeds your own enjoyment, contributing nothing to humanity.

Some come to temples thinking the more incense they burn, the more merit they gain. This is a mistaken view. Burning incense to the Buddha expresses sincerity — one stick is enough. Why use many? With an insincere heart, burning much brings no response. The Buddha does not come to sniff fragrances.

Buddhism does not endorse burning paper money (gilded paper, paper cars and boats; paper clothes, paper shoes, paper goods).

Examine and revise the sutras and texts you translated before. They must be exact, faithful, accordant with the Buddha's intent. That is my wish; I hope you will strive together to complete this mission.

Anger is like water frozen to ice. Melt the ice back to water, for water benefits the myriad things.

Monastics must be dignified in the four deportments — walking, standing, sitting, lying. As the saying goes: walk light as a passing breeze; sit still as a bronze bell; stand straight as a pine; lie curled as a bow.

Cultivation must cultivate the Middle Way. Too much: not the Middle Way. Too little: not the Middle Way either. The Buddha taught the Middle Way's ultimate meaning: falling into neither emptiness nor being.

Without the strength of morality there is no strength of samadhi. Lacking samadhi strength, no wisdom strength can arise. With an unsteady foundation, pillars stand unsure and walls will skew and fall. Morality, samadhi, wisdom are the three flawless studies — missing one, nothing works. Take note of this.

Reciting Namo Amitabha Buddha! Namo Amitabha Buddha! Just the single phrase Namo Amitabha Buddha, with no other false thoughts: that is called using poison to counter poison. Too many false thoughts means too much poison. Death is certain!

Nurture energy; do not get angry (do not give rise to anger)!

You think watching TV, taking phone calls, listening to the radio, playing on computers are fine — but do you know they wound your heart, liver, spleen, lungs, and kidneys? In the future they will make you neither human nor ghost. Come to that, and this world is ruined. So, born in this age when beings are blessed thinly and hard to tame, teaching and transforming them is truly not easy.

The five skandhas are but a kind of yin energy. This yin energy can turn to yang energy. Yin ghosts can also turn to yang ghosts. See whether you know how to transform.

You must keep the Vinaya rules most strictly pure. This is utterly, supremely important.

Lecturing on sutras, lecture on the essentials; do not ramble. Lecture on what bears upon the sutra's text.

Nowadays the whole world talks about qigong. Quite a craze. Qigong comes in many kinds: true and false, proper and deviant. Meeting the deviant, you may go mad — mad beyond even psychiatrists' power to cure.

Do not mistake everyone learning qigong for the proper school. Whoever learns qigong to make money and get rich is deviant — no different from minds stuffed with profit and desire.

The words qigong: name and reality do not match. For energy (qi) has no awareness, so basically it can have no "work" (gong). It should be called spirit work, ghost work, demon work, monster work instead.

Spirit work: the spiritual and bright, gathered in the person (meaning spiritual powers and clear understanding of the truth gather in the person; this line is quoted from the Xici Shang Zhuan, the upper Appended Judgments). Using the strength of holding fast to one proper thought to make spirit govern energy is called qigong. Spirit work also applies effort in mind and intent. Yet, not having reached the ultimate, this school still clings to marks. Spirit work comes when an outer spirit arrives to direct — not energy governing spirit. Spirit work is refined and elegant: when the spirit arrives and possesses, the person does not jump and dance, nor babble nonsense either.

Ghost work differs: when ghosts arrive and possess, the person jumps and dances, laughs and cries, panics uncertainly. This is one of five methods for commanding ghosts. This method sends ghosts into people's bodies — called "flying stars possessing people" — making them babble incoherently. That is because ghosts by nature lack a settled nature and samadhi power.

Demon work and monster work care nothing for reason; they are arrogant, harm people, and specialize in lustful deeds. All qigong is the display of goblins, demons, ghosts, and monsters.

Today's kinds of qigong all carry deviant energy. Originally it should have been righteous energy — taking meditation as food, replete with Dharma joy — for it is a kind of meditative skill. But now, wherever there is qigong, the energy runs truly wild. You tremble and shake, I tremble and shake. Then babbling drivel, all deviant energy. Not a shred of samadhi power; the energy (the qigong master) sends out comes from a scattered mind, yet he claims he has sent out "power" himself, with such and such responses. In truth he has gone mad! Only the mentally ill babble like that.

Two lines judge qigong: The proper person cultivating a deviant dharma turns the deviant dharma proper. The deviant person cultivating the proper Dharma turns the proper Dharma deviant. Not proper means deviant. Not deviant means proper.

Teeth are hard, the tongue is soft: teeth fall, yet the tongue never falls.

Today many are slaves to the body: fine houses to live in, fine cars to ride. Ruled by goods like this — is their own mind truly happy?

Toward the old, the older they are, the more I care for them.

Driving off the glutton-ghosts, lazy-ghosts, sleep-ghosts is the most elementary sitting-meditation skill.

Knowing only others, forgetting yourself — reaching this level is worthy of being called understanding the Buddhadharma.

Recite Guanyin Bodhisattva at all times, in all places. Recite walking, standing, sitting, lying. Silent mental recitation and spoken recitation carry equal merit. So do not compare (the merit of mental versus spoken recitation); recite according to conditions.

Waiting until death to recite Guanyin's name leaves no more chance. Hence the saying: remember impermanence; never indulge.

Whoever you meet surely shares affinities with you. Why quarrel and dispute? Truly pointless.

True Chan meditators are also true Buddha reciters. True Buddha reciters are also true Chan meditators.

The hot-tempered, quick to anger — from morning to night their heads smoke, wrathful energy soaring to the heavens. That, too, shows a lack of virtue.

Good and evil, two roads: cultivate, yet keep creating offenses. If it is the Way, press forward; if it is not the Way, step back. Choose the good road and follow it. In the cauldron of blazing fire, forge a vajra-indestructible body.

To render service, virtue, and words, rely on the six paramitas. The six paramitas are giving, precept-keeping, patience, vigor, meditation, and prajna wisdom.

This world is a world of paper money: just craving this scrap of paper, people forget kindness, righteousness, and morality. Taking coins for real — do you think that deluded or not?

Sitting in meditation means gathering back the outward-bound, scattered mind. This mind has run off somewhere; now we find it and bring it home.

Cultivators who prize spiritual powers are people without understanding.

Free of afflictions, people will harvest treasures.

Watch the fire of ignorance within. This fire of ignorance is like an angry tiger — precisely the offense-roots of past lives.

Guard against the fire of ignorance within: with no fire inside, no fire outside can burn you.

Eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind are called the six thieves. Misusing the six senses turns them into six thieves. Skillful use turns them into Dharma protectors.

Some raise chickens and dogs. When chickens or dogs run off, they chase and catch them back. But when the mind runs off, no one chases it back! That is abandoning the root for the branches: forgetting the root (the mind), gathering the branches (afflictions).

I transmit one key tip to you. What tip? Meeting urgent peril, stay calm; do not get tense and frantic. Set life and death aside, and single-mindedly recite Guanyin Bodhisattva. Peril will surely turn to peace, escaping danger and distress.

True cultivators single-mindedly reciting Guanyin will also gain samadhi. In samadhi, however cold, no cold is felt; however hot, no heat is felt; however hungry or thirsty, no hunger or thirst is felt. Wondrous beyond words.

Give rise to no afflictions; harbor no doubts,

Check yourself; do not touch others.

Admit your many wrongs; argue less,

At ease, pure — and wisdom is born.

Illumined mind: no trial too hard,

Seeing the nature: where is sorrow?

Does the Buddha's light not shine?

Worry, thought, hatred, spite stir it to turmoil.

Cultivating according to this verse, you will surely have special responses.

Reciting Guanyin's name, learn Guanyin's great kindness and great compassion, great joy and great equanimity, great vows and great strength.

DHARMA WORDS

Venerable Master Hsuan Hua

tom_tat: If you want to be free and at ease, you must sweep away the three minds and the four marks. The three minds are the minds that dwell on the present, the past, and the future. These three states of mind have no true reality, so they are called unattainable, impossible to grasp.

If you want to be free and at ease, you must sweep away the three minds and the four marks. The three minds are the minds that think about the present, the past, and the future. These three states of mind have no true reality, so they are called unattainable — impossible to grasp.

Why is it that only sages enjoy freedom and ease? Because sages have no four marks: no notion of self, no notion of others, no notion of living beings, no notion of a life span. Therefore they attain freedom.

Why are we deluded and unenlightened? Because we have been poisoned too deeply by greed, anger, and delusion. That is why we cannot awaken.

In the Proper Dharma Age, everyone cultivates. In the Dharma-Ending Age, no one cultivates. If everyone cultivates now, the Dharma-Ending Age will turn into the Proper Dharma Age.

The law of cause and effect is: giving rise to delusion (the mind stirring with false thoughts and confusion), leading to creating karma (body, speech, and mind producing actions, words, and thoughts), ending in undergoing retribution (body, speech, and mind bearing the consequences of what was done).

From life to death: a human lifetime. This body is like foam drifting here and there on the water's surface — truly illusory, unreal, vanishing in an instant. Why cling to it? Why be attached?

Without seeking the Way, you cannot escape the road of delusion. To leave the road of delusion, you must cultivate the Way.

Human life is impermanent; careers are impermanent; wealth and honor are impermanent too. As the saying goes: joy is the cause of suffering. All worldly joy and pleasure conceal suffering within.

Why can we not concentrate singlemindedly on reciting Guanyin's name? Because we cannot gather in the six senses — ear, eye, nose, tongue, body, and mind — nor rein in these six thieves. So they stir up wind and waves at will, and false thoughts flare up. The mind can never be still; it keeps reaching outward, making trouble for itself.

To awaken, you must sit in meditation. Sitting in meditation means no longer being deluded: it is the road out of the three realms.

Because monastics regard sutra recitation lightly (emphasizing offerings, rites, and ceremonies instead of actual cultivation and realization), each generation is worse than the last. They nurture habits of greed for food and laziness. This is truly a misfortune for Buddhism. If this wrong view is not corrected in time, the future of Buddhism is hard to imagine.

For the benefit of the whole world, recite Guanyin's name. Help the world erase disasters. In everything you do, do not think only of yourself.

In heaven and earth, all things ceaselessly arise and endlessly transform (arising, changing, never stopping) because of the Buddha nature. Without the Buddha nature, everything would perish. (All relative phenomena exist only within the scope of the absolute nature.)

Where do people come from? Some say humans evolved from monkeys. But where did monkeys come from? If monkeys could turn into humans, why don't they keep turning into humans now? Strange indeed!

Some people cannot live a single day without gossiping; a day without lying leaves them restless, as if they had not eaten. Morning and night they live off gossip and lies. Don't you find that strange? It is truly hard to understand.

Nowadays some cultivators like to live alone in a small house (a hut). Why? Because they do not keep the Vinaya rules. With no one watching, breaking the precepts goes unnoticed. They do as they please, with no one to restrain them — free and easy, bound by nothing. Then they gather laypeople for this rite and that ceremony: in truth they are just using the Buddha (hiding behind cultivation) to get food and clothing.

The merit of holding and reciting the Great Compassion Mantra not only repels thieves and robbers but also cures a hundred illnesses and dispels demonic trials. Therefore we should sincerely hold and recite it.

Wherever the Flower Adornment Sutra is, there the Buddha is. It is like a brilliant cloud shining everywhere throughout the great trichiliocosm.

The noble person has a teaching that can reform destiny. Destiny is made by oneself; blessings are sought from oneself. Doing no evil, a bad destiny will naturally turn good. Doing no good, only evil, a good destiny will also turn bad. Destiny shifts and changes; it does not bind people rigidly with no freedom left. Do not be superstitious (about destiny being fixed and prearranged).

The master only leads the disciple to the door of the Way. Whether you cultivate is up to each person.

The Pure Land method suits the faculties of everyone. Using little effort to gain great success. It truly is a Dharma door in accord with the truth, suited to all faculties.

Buddha sounds like the words bất đại — "not great"! The Buddha is no greater than anyone and no smaller than anyone. So bất đại ("not great") is precisely the Buddha!

Cultivators of the Way must not quarrel. For example, in the Buddha hall those who come later stand behind; those who came first stand ahead. One who arrives late should not say: "I wear the sash, so I must stand in front of those who don't. I must push them down below." That is called contending.

To be parents is to repay debts. To be children is to collect debts. Living beings do not understand this, so they take (the parent-child bond) to be great joy.

At birth, our hands are empty. At death, our hands are empty too. We can bring nothing with us. Nor can we stay.

Judaism is also Buddhism; Christianity is also Buddhism. The names change but the meaning does not. I do not regard religions as religions. I see that religions are only transformations of human nature. So whatever religion I meet, I belong to that religion. I have no religion of my own.

The Chinese word for busy is made of the characters mind and lost (gone) put together. It looks just like the word forget, which is also mind plus lost put together. So being busy means being so busy you lose your mind altogether — so busy you completely forget your true mind!

How should you cultivate? First, cut off desires and sever emotional love. Do not stay too far from people, but do not get too close either. Too distant, and you lose good affinities with others. Too close, and sentiment rules reason, making cultivation impossible.

In cultivation you must not wear masks, pretend, or put on a play for others to watch. Cultivation depends entirely on your own skill. Only thus will there be results. With a measure of sincerity comes a measure of response. Everything depends on a sincere heart, true and undeceiving. Never cheat yourself or cheat others.

To save the world, you cannot use atomic bombs, hydrogen bombs, or lasers, for they are things that destroy the world. You can only use the eight virtues: filial devotion, fraternity, loyalty, trustworthiness, propriety, righteousness, integrity, and honor. These eight virtues are the elixir that rescues the souls of living beings, the most effective medicine to save people's lives.

The world's incurable, terminal illness is: the bankruptcy of education.

Someone says: "I am the real Buddha!" Ah! If you are the real Buddha, then who is the fake Buddha? Just like the president — he never says, "I am the real president!" If he did, then who would be the fake president? From this we can infer: whenever someone claims something is "real," there is surely something wrong.

Do all good deeds: that is, cultivate pure conduct. Without purity, it is not goodness. Purity itself is goodness.

You think vegetarians may eat eggs? Sure! Just wait until you are reborn as a chicken — then you will understand (a chicken's fate) comes precisely from eating chicken eggs.

If you cannot cut off sexual desire, then even if you leave home for eighty thousand great eons, you will only waste your time and create offenses within Buddhism.

A tree without roots will wither. A person without roots must die.

Whatever illness or pain, it is all due to karmic creditors coming to collect debts. What is illness? Illness is also a way of preaching the Dharma, helping people see that this body is suffering, that birth, aging, sickness, and death are suffering. It can come to you at any time. It sends you telegrams, phone calls, or letters to remind you (in the form of suffering from illness). Not only can you fall ill — one day you must die.

With birth comes aging, then illness, then death. This process teaches us to know the suffering of the chain of birth, aging, sickness, and death, so that we prepare for liberation and are no longer bound by destiny. Therefore no matter what illness you have, you must bring forth the resolve for enlightenment (bodhicitta), give rise to awakening, and see all things as impermanent, suffering, truly empty, and selfless. If you can do that, then illness is also a good thing.

One who knows the Buddhadharma does not contend, does not crave, does not seek, is not selfish, does not pursue self-benefit, and does not lie. Things like the five eyes, the six spiritual powers, and so on are all superfluous — to cultivate while seeking them is like climbing a tree to find fish.

If you young people memorize the Shurangama Sutra fluently, you will certainly develop great wisdom and gain unobstructed eloquence.

In the Dharma-Ending Age, people in white (laypeople) openly accept offerings and propagate the Buddhadharma. White-clad means laypeople. They openly chant for the dead, perform rites to cross over the departed, and read fortune sticks. They use Buddhism to earn food and clothing.

Ghosts only feed on the essence of offerings; they have no need of money or food. If you have money, do some meritorious deed and transfer the merit to the departed spirits. If you buy paper cars, paper money, paper airplanes, paper houses... to burn as offerings, that is delusion in the extreme.

Once paper money is burned to ash, how do you know whether it has any effect? If you say burning it does have an effect (that the dead can use the money you burn), then Westerners, whose relatives never burn paper money for them — have they all become poor, destitute ghosts? Could it be: in the West there are no poor ghosts, in the East no rich gods!

All my life, I have never wanted to chant for the dead, perform the Flaming Mouth rite, or hold Water-Land Dharma assemblies, because I lack virtue. My Way is not enough to move people; my virtue is not enough to teach anyone. I have not yet crossed myself over — how could I cross over departed souls? That is why I do not have the courage to do such things.

The Buddha-recitation method: the old, with few years left, should best recite the Buddha's name. The young, with long lives ahead, are also suited to reciting the Buddha's name. The middle-aged, having clearly experienced all the world's ways, should also recite the Buddha's name. The sick, not knowing when they will die, must urgently recite the Buddha's name. When not sick, while the body is still strong, it is best to recite the Buddha's name.

Everyone should rectify the mind and cultivate the self. A rectified mind means no scattered, jumbled thoughts, no thoughts of improper things. When the mind is upright, ghosts will not come looking for you. It is like a cat's bowl of food swarming with flies — that is because the food is too filthy. Without that bowl, no flies would come. Whatever your mind is like, it will attract its like. Ghosts do not come from outside; it is the defiled mind within that invites them.

Without meeting demons, how can you see through the mortal world? Without enduring suffering, how can you resolve to truly cultivate? Do not let a clever mind fool you into thinking you know everything. In truth you know nothing. When a state comes, it shakes you until your hands and feet flail in panic!

After receiving the precepts, you must act as envoys of the Buddha's house, as troops of Buddhism, as great generals, great heroes, great stalwarts in Buddhism. Do not be careless and casual, drifting with bad habits, fooling around day after day, looking nothing like one who has just received the precepts.

Do not be scattered: meeting everyone with flattering greetings while applying no effort to your own cultivation. You must know how to cultivate: talking too much is not good. The noble and wealthy do not talk much. Talking much makes one's character lowly. The lowly have no value. The noble speak slowly — so it is.

Within the law of cause and effect, the offense of sexual misconduct is the most serious. Its punishment is even more dreadful: for every act of sexual misconduct in life, after death the body will be sawed from head to foot that many times with a great saw. One who married a hundred times in life will be sawed a hundred times after death.

Because we cannot see through and cannot let go, we get tangled and bound up in conditioned dharmas and unconditioned dharmas, in things with marks and things without marks. Unable to see clearly (the present state or experience, or the unchanging truth), we keep dragging our feet (as if wading through mud). Within the six paths of rebirth, birth and death go on and on.

Reading the Shurangama Sutra develops wisdom. Reading the Dharma Flower Sutra leads to Buddhahood. Hence: wisdom comes from the Shurangama; Buddhahood from the Dharma Flower. The Flower Adornment Sutra returns to the source: all beings flow out from this Dharma Realm, and all will return to the Dharma Realm. Choose the sutra you feel happiest with — that is what suits your faculties. Once you have a compatible teaching, study it; do not spend every day chasing money and forgetting the Buddhadharma.

The great matter in one's life: taking refuge in the Triple Jewel.

Taking refuge in the Triple Jewel rests on two words: sincerity. Without sincerity, you go through the motions, careless and irresponsible, with no response at all.

Each morning when you wake, face the Buddha and make four vows. Every Bodhisattva makes these four vows. Each night, examine yourself: Boundless beings, I vow to save them — have I saved anyone? If not, hurry up and save them. Endless afflictions, I vow to end them — have I ended them? If not, end them. Countless Dharma doors, I vow to learn them — have I learned them? If not, find free moments amid a busy day to read some sutras and Buddhist books. The unsurpassed Buddha Way, I vow to realize it — I am still an ordinary person, not yet a Buddha; I must quickly cultivate in order to become one.

Buddhist learners should not roam about. Running from temple to temple all life long, they gain nothing in the end: they cannot lecture on sutras, cannot recite the Buddha's name, cannot perform repentance rites either.

Seeking out a good spiritual teacher: even among monastics, dragons and snakes are mixed together, hard to tell apart. If you stray into a side door or deviant path, it is truly dangerous. If you mistakenly follow a deviant teacher preaching the Dharma, the danger is even greater.

In the temple, talk about things connected with Buddhist principle and cultivation. Do not talk about this person this way, that person that way — all gossip. The more you talk, the more you fall. The more you fall, the harder it is to study the Buddhadharma. Why do you hold mantras and keep forgetting? Because you are too scattered. Why do you recite sutras without remembering? Because you are too scattered.

If you know how to listen, then even when I scold people, you will hear wonderful Dharma. Even when I hit people, you will see it as a timely awakening. If you do not know how to listen, then whatever blessing or help I give you, you will find meaningless and unreasonable.

If you want me to fly to heaven: nothing hard about it. Teaching Americans is the hardest.

If you want me to burrow into the earth: nothing hard about it. Teaching Americans is the hardest.

If you want a rooster to lay eggs: nothing hard about it. Teaching Americans is the hardest.

You think being bowed to makes you remarkable? Ask yourself: what virtue do I have? What wisdom? Am I worthy of others' reverence? Worthy of their worship? Always turn the light around and reflect on yourself like this.

When making offerings to monastics, you need the eye that recognizes truth (the Dharma-discerning eye). Offer to cultivators who are pure in conduct.

The Buddha spoke the Tripitaka, the twelve divisions of sutras — all for one purpose: to smash people's attachments. Yet we refuse to heed the Buddha's teaching and instead act as traitors: clinging forever to the SELF.

When I came, I had nothing. When I leave, I want nothing. I want to leave no trace in this world. I came from empty space, and I shall return to empty space.

THE END
